sections.title: How the wedge influences the final shell geometry
sections.body:
The wedge does more than affect how two pieces of timber meet.

It changes where the inside and outside surfaces of the finished dome end up.

That matters once we stop thinking about the frame as a collection of centerlines and start thinking about actual wood, actual panels, actual insulation, and an actual weather surface.

A geodesic calculator can give us a network of ideal points and straight chord lengths.

That is enough to define the mathematical frame.

It is not enough to define the finished shell.

The wedge adds thickness and taper around those lines.

Once that happens, the dome has several different surfaces instead of one.

GEOMETRY

At minimum, we need to distinguish between:

* the theoretical geodesic geometry,
* the interior structural surface,
* the exterior structural surface,
* the panel or sheathing surface,
* and the final weather surface.

Those surfaces are offset from one another.

They do not necessarily have the same radius.

They also do not necessarily use identical triangle dimensions.

That distinction becomes important as soon as the wedge has enough thickness to matter.

THEORETICAL GEOMETRY

The cleanest mathematical model starts with vertices located on a defined sphere.

Straight lines connect those vertices.

Those straight lines are the geodesic chords.

If we stopped there, every member would have zero thickness.

The model would tell us:

* where the vertices are,
* how long the chords are,
* which triangles exist,
* and how the triangular faces meet.

That is the skeleton of the dome.

The wedge is physical material wrapped around that skeleton.

Once we add the real timber, one side of the member lies closer to the dome center and another lies farther away.

That immediately creates more than one envelope.

THE INSIDE ENVELOPE

The narrow side of the wedge faces inward.

If we connect those narrow faces around the dome, they create an interior structural envelope.

That envelope is not automatically the same surface as the theoretical geodesic sphere.

Its exact location depends on where the wedge is positioned relative to the theoretical chord.

For example, if the mathematical chord passes through the center of the timber section, then part of the wedge lies inside that line and part lies outside it.

If the chord is aligned with another datum, such as a bolt-center line or interior reference face, then the offsets change.

That is why the physical datum has to be fixed before final dimensions are generated.

THE OUTSIDE ENVELOPE

The wide side of the wedge creates the exterior structural envelope.

Because the member widens toward the outside, the exterior edge occupies a larger local envelope than the interior edge.

This is part of what makes the wedge useful.

It gives the structure a controlled transition from a smaller interior perimeter to a larger exterior perimeter.

But it also means that an exterior panel cannot automatically be cut to the same dimensions as an interior panel.

The outside triangle is physically farther from the dome center.

Its edges may therefore have different finished dimensions depending on how the panel lands on the wedge.

ONE TRIANGLE, MULTIPLE TRIANGLES

A single geodesic face can produce several different physical triangle outlines.

We can think of them as:

1. the theoretical triangle,
2. the interior wedge-face triangle,
3. the exterior wedge-face triangle,
4. the exterior panel triangle,
5. the finished weather-surface triangle.

Those outlines may be close to one another.

They are not automatically identical.

This becomes especially important in larger members or thick insulated assemblies.

If the difference is ignored, gaps can appear where panels meet.

Edges can overhang.

Fastener locations can move away from the intended framing.

A panel that fits perfectly on a computer-generated theoretical triangle may not fit the actual outside of the timber frame.

THE WEDGE AS AN OFFSET GENERATOR

A useful way to think about the wedge is that it generates an offset between the interior and exterior shell geometry.

Suppose the distance from the inside face of the wedge to the outside face is:

$$
t
$$

That thickness moves the exterior surface outward from the interior surface.

At the same time, the wedge widens from:

$$
w_i
$$

to:

$$
w_o
$$

The width difference is:

$$
\Delta w=w_o-w_i
$$

The wedge therefore changes the shell in two directions at once.

It moves the exterior surface outward.

It also spreads the neighboring face edges apart.

That means the shell is not created by simply taking the interior triangle and moving it outward by one constant dimension.

The face plane moves outward, and the edge geometry changes with it.

This is why a full three-dimensional model becomes useful.

FACE PLANES

Each triangular face can be represented as a plane.

The neighboring face has another plane.

Those two planes intersect along their shared edge.

The wedge occupies space around that edge.

If the wide surfaces of the wedge are intended to support exterior paneling, then the outside panel planes have to agree with the wedge geometry.

There are several possible ways to handle this.

One approach is to shape the wedge so its side faces directly establish the neighboring panel planes.

Another approach is to let the panels sit on another prepared surface.

Another is to use battens, spacers, clips, or a secondary frame over the wedge structure.

Each approach creates a different shell geometry.

The important part is that the relationship is deliberate.

A panel should not be forced into whatever space remains after the frame is built.

THE PANEL CONTACT SURFACE

If a sheet panel sits directly on the wide side of the wedge, we need to know exactly what surface supports it.

The panel may bear on:

* the entire exterior face,
* a narrow flat land,
* a rabbet,
* a machined seat,
* a secondary strip,
* or a separate panel frame.

That contact surface becomes part of the shell datum.

Once it is defined, the panel dimensions can be derived from it.

Without that definition, the phrase "exterior panel size" is incomplete.

The geometry depends on where the panel actually sits.

PANEL THICKNESS

The panel itself also has thickness.

A plywood skin, fiberglass panel, composite panel, or insulated assembly adds another offset outside the structural frame.

If the panel thickness is:

$$
p
$$

then the finished exterior surface lies farther outward than the panel-support surface.

If another weather layer is added, that creates another offset.

This means the finished weather radius can be larger than the structural radius used for the original geodesic calculation.

That is not a problem.

It simply has to be understood.

The reference diameter of the dome should always state which surface it describes.

A "20-foot dome" could refer to:

* theoretical vertex diameter,
* structural centerline diameter,
* inside structural diameter,
* outside structural diameter,
* panel-support diameter,
* or finished exterior diameter.

Those are different measurements once the structure has real thickness.

PANEL SEAMS

The wedge also affects what happens where panels meet.

Two flat panels on neighboring faces approach each other at an angle.

Their edges can be handled several ways.

They may:

* butt together,
* leave a controlled gap,
* overlap,
* receive an exterior cap,
* receive a gasket,
* sit inside a channel,
* or meet against a cover strip.

The wedge can help create the space required for that joint.

For example, a wider exterior portion may allow a panel edge to land fully on timber while leaving room for a seam cover or gasket.

The amount of usable exterior bearing width therefore becomes part of the panel-joint design.

A narrow wedge may fit the geometry but provide too little practical panel attachment area.

A wider wedge may improve the interface but use more material.

That is another example of geometry and construction requirements meeting in the same part.

THREE-MEMBER TRIANGLE

Take one triangular wedge frame.

On the interior side, the three narrow edges define one perimeter.

On the exterior side, the three wider edges define another.

If the wedge profiles are symmetrical and consistent, the exterior envelope expands around the triangle.

A panel attached outside the frame therefore follows the exterior triangle, not the interior one.

That sounds obvious once the physical member is visible.

It becomes easy to miss when working from a line drawing where every strut is represented by one thin line.

This is why the book should show the same triangle in several layers.

The reader should be able to see:

the chord triangle,

the timber triangle,

and the panel triangle.

THE SHELL DOES NOT HAVE TO FOLLOW THE WEDGE DIRECTLY

DESIGN VARIATION

The exterior shell does not have to sit directly on the wedge.

A secondary shell system can be added outside the frame.

For example, the wedge frame could support:

* furring strips,
* panel clips,
* an offset rail,
* a secondary triangular frame,
* insulation blocks,
* or another attachment system.

That can create a more continuous exterior surface.

It can also decouple the structural wedge geometry from the final weather skin.

This may be useful if:

* the wedge is optimized for structure,
* the panel needs a larger bearing surface,
* exterior insulation is added,
* removable panels are desired,
* or the shell needs a drainage cavity.

The tradeoff is additional material and another layer of geometry to manage.

The cleanest system is not automatically the one with the fewest layers.

It is the one where every layer has a defined job and a defined reference.

INTERIOR FINISH

The same problem exists on the inside.

If interior finish is attached directly to the narrow faces, those narrow faces define the interior panel geometry.

If a secondary interior frame is added, the visible interior surface moves inward.

That can change:

* interior diameter,
* usable floor area near the wall,
* window and door trim,
* utility routing,
* and the relationship between the interior finish and the structural frame.

The shell should therefore be thought of as a layered system.

The wedge is one layer.

It influences the others.

INSULATION

An insulated dome can place material:

* between wedge members,
* outside the frame,
* inside the frame,
* inside panel assemblies,
* or in combinations of these locations.

Each approach changes the final shell thickness.

If insulation fills the space between neighboring wedge frames, the face geometry of that cavity matters.

If insulation is continuous outside the frame, then panel clips or secondary members may move the weather shell farther outward.

If insulation is inside the structure, the interior envelope moves inward.

The geometry of the building should therefore be tracked through the complete wall section rather than only through the strut centerlines.

DOORS AND WINDOWS

Openings make these offsets more obvious.

A door frame or window frame has to pass through some portion of the shell thickness.

If the structure has:

* wedge frame,
* exterior panel,
* insulation,
* weather layer,
* interior finish,

then the opening detail has to connect all of those surfaces.

The frame depth cannot be designed from the theoretical geodesic line alone.

The real shell has thickness.

That shell thickness may also vary depending on whether a secondary panel system is used.

Special opening modules should therefore reference the actual finished wall section.

BASE GEOMETRY

The wedge can also influence the base of the dome.

At the bottom course, the exterior structural envelope and interior structural envelope may intersect the floor or foundation at different locations.

That can affect:

* base plates,
* floor edge details,
* flashing,
* exterior drainage,
* insulation transitions,
* and anchor locations.

If the mathematical base ring is defined only by chord centerlines, the physical timber can extend inward or outward from that ring.

That extension needs to be accounted for when the floor and foundation are designed.

Otherwise the frame may be mathematically correct while the physical base does not land where the foundation detail expects it.

SHELL SMOOTHNESS

The wedge does not turn the geodesic dome into a continuously curved surface.

The shell is still made from flat or nearly flat triangular faces unless another curved skin system is added.

The wedge influences how those flat faces meet.

It can make the transition between faces cleaner and more controlled.

Increasing dome frequency still reduces the size of the facets.

The wedge does not replace frequency.

It works within the chosen frequency.

A low-frequency dome with wedge members still has large visible triangular faces.

A higher-frequency dome still uses smaller facets.

The wedge helps define the physical edge between them.

FABRICATION ERROR AND SHELL FIT

Errors in wedge geometry can show up dramatically at the shell.

Suppose the wedge is slightly too narrow on the outside.

One isolated member may not look badly wrong.

But when panels are installed, the joint may close more tightly than intended.

If the wedge is too wide, a seam may open.

If the profile varies along the member, the panel gap may change from one end to the other.

If the wedge twists, the supporting surface may no longer remain in the intended panel plane.

This gives us another inspection method.

The wedge can be checked as an individual part.

But a completed triangular frame or sample panel assembly can reveal whether the combined geometry actually produces the intended shell surfaces.

BUILD NOTE

Before committing to a complete dome shell, the reference build should include a full-scale mockup of at least two neighboring triangular faces.

That mockup should include:

* actual wedge members,
* the actual connection,
* the intended exterior panel material,
* the intended seam or gasket,
* and enough surrounding structure to reproduce the real face-to-face angle.

The mockup can then be checked for:

* panel bearing,
* seam width,
* fastener access,
* edge alignment,
* exterior continuity,
* interior clearance,
* and whether the panels sit naturally without being forced.

A three-dimensional mockup can expose problems that do not appear in a flat panel drawing.

That is especially valuable before producing an entire dome worth of panels.

TOLERANCE STACK-UP

Shell geometry also gives us a reason to track cumulative error.

Imagine a panel system where every wedge is slightly too wide on the exterior.

One joint may absorb the error.

Several repeated joints can move the final position of a distant vertex or cause the last panel in a course to fit poorly.

The same can happen with panel dimensions.

A small seam-width error repeated around a ring can become a large closure error.

For that reason, tolerances should eventually be assigned to the complete assembly instead of only to individual pieces.

Useful checks can include:

* individual wedge profile,
* completed triangle dimensions,
* distance between known vertices,
* panel seam width,
* course circumference or polygon dimensions,
* and closure error at a known reference point.

The part tolerance and the assembly tolerance solve different problems.

DESIGN VARIATION

The wedge can also be deliberately modified to create shell features.

Possible variations include:

* a wider outside face for more panel bearing,
* a rabbet for panel edges,
* a groove for a gasket,
* a drainage channel,
* a removable cover strip,
* a clip attachment,
* a secondary insulation seat,
* or an interior finish seat.

Each added feature changes the physical member.

That feature should therefore be included in the member drawing rather than added casually during installation.

A structural wedge with a panel rabbet is a different manufactured part from a plain wedge of the same overall size.

EXPERIMENTAL

A more developed version of the system could treat the wedge as an interface between structure and replaceable shell panels.

The frame could remain permanent while exterior triangular panels are mechanically attached to standardized wedge edges.

A damaged panel could then potentially be replaced without replacing the frame.

Opaque, transparent, insulated, or specialized utility panels could share a common edge interface.

This depends heavily on the final joint design.

Weather sealing, structural contribution, drainage, tolerances, panel restraint, and long-term movement would all have to be developed and tested.

The geometry makes the concept possible.

It does not prove the finished enclosure system.

SAFETY / ENGINEERING

The shell can also participate structurally depending on how it is built.

A thin nonstructural cover attached to a complete frame is different from a structural panel intended to transfer load between members.

The same is true for:

* plywood skins,
* composite panels,
* stressed skins,
* diaphragms,
* insulated structural panels,
* and mechanically connected shells.

If the enclosure contributes to structural performance, its fasteners, edge conditions, material properties, openings, and load path require engineering appropriate to that system.

The wedge shape alone does not establish shell capacity.

REFERENCE BUILD

For the 20-foot 2V reference dome, the shell should eventually be modeled as a set of separate but related surfaces.

At minimum:

$$
S_0 = \text{theoretical geodesic/chord geometry}
$$

$$
S_1 = \text{interior structural surface}
$$

$$
S_2 = \text{exterior structural/panel-support surface}
$$

$$
S_3 = \text{exterior panel surface}
$$

$$
S_4 = \text{finished weather surface}
$$

An interior finish surface can be added separately if required.

The exact offsets between those surfaces will depend on the final wedge size and enclosure design.

Once those layers are defined, we can generate different dimensions for different jobs.

The strut cut list comes from the structural geometry.

The exterior panel cut list comes from the panel-support geometry.

The floor interface comes from the physical base geometry.

The window and door depth comes from the complete shell section.

The finished outside diameter comes from the weather surface.

Those are all parts of the same dome.

They are not the same measurement.

That is the main way the wedge influences the shell.

It takes the dome from a network of mathematical lines and gives that network thickness.

Once the frame has thickness, every layer attached to it needs its own defined geometry.

chapters.title: 3. Understanding Dome Geometry
chapters.body:
The wedge method is a way of building a dome, but a dome is a shape first and a method second. This chapter is the shape.

None of it is specific to wedges. Everything here is true of any 2V dome built by anybody out of anything, and if you have built one before you can skim it. What you cannot skip is the last section but one, on dihedral angles, because the whole method rests on a number that appears there and does not appear anywhere else.
chapters.notes:
CHAPTER GOAL: Build a practical, illustrated chapter covering 3. Understanding Dome Geometry.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Radius and diameter
sections.body:
Everything in a geodesic dome is measured from one point that is not there.

The centre of the sphere. On the reference build it sits on the floor, in the
middle of the room, and nothing is bolted to it. But every vertex in the frame
is exactly the same distance from it, and that distance is the only number the
whole design really has.

On the reference build that number is 116.4984 inches. Call it a radius of
nine feet eight and a half.

The dome is a hemisphere, so the diameter across the floor is twice that:
19.416 feet. Nineteen feet five. And because it is a hemisphere and not a
taller or shorter slice, the height is the same as the radius: 9.708 feet.

Those three numbers are not three decisions. They are one decision, written
three ways.

WHERE THE RADIUS ACTUALLY COMES FROM

Here is the part that surprises people, and it is worth getting straight
before anything else.

You do not choose the radius.

You choose the longest stick you are willing to cut, and the radius falls out
of it.

On the reference build the longest member is six feet. Seventy-two inches.
That is not a geometric choice at all -- it is a decision about what fits on a
truck, what one person can carry, and what comes out of the log you have. From
that, the geometry gives you a radius of 116.4984 inches, and from the radius
you get the diameter, the height, the floor area, and every other stick in the
building.

Six feet in, nineteen feet five out.

If you want a bigger dome you do not scale the radius. You pick a longer stick
and let the radius follow. That is the direction the arithmetic runs, and
people who try to run it the other way end up with a beautiful radius and a
member length nobody can cut.

WHAT THE RADIUS DOES NOT TELL YOU

The radius is the distance to the vertices. It is not the distance to the
skin, and it is not the distance to the inside face of the wall.

A member on this dome is six inches deep. It sits with its outer face near the
sphere and its inner face six inches closer to the middle. So the room inside
is smaller than the sphere by roughly the depth of the wall, everywhere.

That sounds obvious written down. It stops being obvious at two in the
afternoon when you are trying to work out whether a piece of furniture fits,
and you measure from a drawing of the sphere rather than from the inside of
the wood.

Measure the room. Not the maths.

sections.title: Sphere versus dome
sections.body:
A geodesic sphere is a closed ball of triangles. A geodesic dome is the part
of one you kept.

That is the whole distinction, and it matters more than it sounds.

The reference build is a hemisphere: exactly half a sphere, cut on the
equator. It sits on the ground on ten flat feet and the cut is level all the
way round.

WHY A HEMISPHERE AND NOT SOMETHING ELSE

You can cut a 2V sphere at the equator and you get a clean edge. Ten base
vertices, all at the same height, all level. Nothing has to be shimmed and
nothing is left hanging.

Cut it anywhere else and you do not get that. A three-eighths dome or a
five-eighths dome means cutting through triangles rather than between them,
and every one of those cuts is a new angle, a new length, and a new
opportunity to be wrong.

The hemisphere is the cut the geometry offers you for free. The reference
build takes it.

WHAT YOU GIVE UP

Honesty first: a hemisphere is not the most useful shape for a house.

The wall at the bottom is already leaning in. Stand at the edge of a
nineteen-foot dome and the ceiling is at your shoulder. The floor area says
277 square feet, but the floor area you can stand upright on is considerably
less than that, and a wardrobe against the wall does not fit against the wall.

A taller cut -- five-eighths of a sphere rather than a half -- gives you a
straighter wall and more usable room. It also gives you a base ring that is no
longer level, a set of triangles that are no longer the two families you know,
and a lot of new arithmetic.

The reference build chooses the easy cut and pays for it in headroom near the
edge. If you want the other trade, the geometry will do it. You will just be
solving a different dome.

THE FLOOR IS NOT A CIRCLE

One more thing that catches people.

The base of a 2V hemisphere is not round. It is a ten-sided polygon, because
there are ten base vertices and straight members between them.

The circle that would pass through those ten corners encloses 296 square feet.
The decagon actually enclosed by the members encloses 277.

Nineteen square feet of difference. Not enough to matter for most things, and
exactly enough to matter if you are buying flooring or pouring a slab and you
measured the circle.

sections.title: Frequency
sections.body:
Frequency is how many times you cut each edge of the original shape before you
push the points out onto the sphere.

That is it. That is the whole idea.

Start with an icosahedron -- twenty triangles, the most round thing you can
make out of identical flat faces. Leave it alone and you have a 1V dome:
twenty big triangles, very angular, very cheap, and not very round.

Cut every edge in half and you get a 2V. Each original triangle becomes four
smaller ones. Push all the new points out until they sit on the sphere, and
the shape gets rounder.

Cut every edge in three and you get a 3V. Each triangle becomes nine. Rounder
again.

Higher frequency means more triangles, smaller triangles, more sticks, more
joints, and a shape closer to a true sphere.

WHAT FREQUENCY COSTS

Every step up in frequency is a step up in parts count, and the parts count
goes up faster than the roundness does.

A 2V hemisphere has 65 edges. A 3V has substantially more, and every one of
them is a stick to cut, a joint to make, and a place to be out by a sixteenth.

The reference build is a 2V because 2V is where the parts count stops being
absurd and the shape is still round enough to behave like a dome. Forty
triangles. Sixty-five edges. Twenty-six vertices. Those are numbers a person
can hold.

If you are building something forty feet across, 2V will give you triangles
too big to panel sensibly and you will want 3V. If you are building a
greenhouse over a vegetable bed, 1V is probably enough and you should not let
anyone talk you into more.

THE PART NOBODY MENTIONS

Frequency does not change how hard the *joints* are. It changes how many of
them there are.

A 3V dome is not a harder dome to build than a 2V. It is the same difficulty,
more times. If your 2V joints are coming out clean, your 3V joints will too.
If they are not, going up a frequency will not fix them -- it will just give
you more of them to be unhappy about.

Get the 2V right first.

sections.title: 1V, 2V, 3V, and higher frequencies
sections.body:
Here is what each one actually gives you, in the terms that matter on a build
site rather than in a geometry textbook.

1V

Twenty triangles in a full sphere, ten in a hemisphere. All of them identical.

This is the only frequency where every single strut is the same length, and
that is a genuinely large advantage. One cut list. One jig setting. No A and
B members to keep separated.

It is also barely a dome. The faces are large and flat, the shape is
noticeably faceted, and the span you can cover before the members get absurdly
long is small. Fine for a play structure, a chicken coop, a garden cover.

2V

Forty triangles in the hemisphere the reference build uses. Two strut lengths,
called A and B.

This is the first frequency that looks like a dome and behaves like one, and
it is the last frequency where the parts count is small enough to keep in your
head. Sixty-five edges, twenty-six vertices, 120 physical members once every
triangle owns its own three sticks.

The two lengths are the price of admission. You will cut sixty of one and
sixty of the other and you will mix them up at least once.

3V AND UP

Three strut lengths at 3V, more above that. Rounder, stronger for its weight,
better at spanning distance.

Also: substantially more sticks, more joints, more sorting, and a much higher
cost to any systematic error. If your jig is out by a degree at 2V you will
notice at the last panel. At 4V you will notice at the last twelve panels, and
you will have already cut them.

WHAT THIS BOOK ASSUMES

Everything from here on assumes 2V unless it says otherwise.

Not because 2V is the best frequency. Because it is the frequency where the
wedge method can be explained completely, built by one person, and checked
without a computer -- and because everything that is true about a wedge at 2V
is still true at 3V, with more of it.

Learn the method at 2V. Go up a frequency when the span demands it, not
because higher numbers sound better.

sections.title: Chord lengths
sections.body:
A chord is the straight line between two vertices.

It is not the curve of the sphere. The sphere curves; your timber does not.
Every member in the frame is a straight chord cutting across the inside of a
curved surface, and the dome is round only in the sense that enough straight
lines arranged carefully look round from a distance.

THE TWO CHORDS ON THIS DOME

A 2V dome has two of them. The book calls them A and B, and so does everyone
else.

On the reference build:

* A is 72.000 inches -- six feet, the longest member
* B is 63.670 inches -- five feet three and eleven-sixteenths

There are sixty of each in the frame.

CHORD FACTORS

The lengths above are for one dome at one size. The numbers that travel are
the chord factors: the chord divided by the sphere radius.

* A factor: 0.618034
* B factor: 0.546533

Multiply either by your radius and you have your member length. That is the
whole calculation, and it is the same calculation for every 2V dome that has
ever been built.

The A factor is worth a second look. 0.618034 is the golden ratio minus one,
and it is not a coincidence -- it falls out of the icosahedron the dome is
subdivided from. You do not need to care why. You do need to type it
correctly.

GOING THE OTHER WAY

Most people do not start with a radius. They start with the longest stick they
can get.

Divide it by 0.618034 and you have your radius. From there, multiply by
0.546533 for the B chord and you have your second length.

Seventy-two inches divided by 0.618034 is 116.4984 inches. Times 0.546533 is
63.670 inches. That is the reference build, derived from one decision about
timber.

WHAT THE CHORD IS NOT

The chord is the distance between vertex points -- the mathematical corners,
floating in space.

It is not the length of wood you cut.

Your actual sticks come out shorter than the chord, because the ends get
trimmed back where they meet other members, and how much shorter depends on
how the joint is made. On the reference build the A members come off the saw
between 68.977 and 70.182 inches of usable stock against a 72.000 inch chord.

That gap between the chord and the stick is where most first-dome errors live.
It has its own chapter.

sections.title: A/B/C strut families
sections.body:
A strut family is a set of members that are all the same length and all do the
same job. Domes are described by how many families they have.

A 2V dome has two: A and B. A 3V has three, usually called A, B and C. A 1V
has one.

WHAT A AND B ACTUALLY ARE ON THIS DOME

A members are the longer ones. Sixty of them, 72.000 inches of chord.

B members are the shorter ones. Sixty of them, 63.670 inches of chord.

They are not scattered at random. They sit in a pattern, and the pattern is
worth learning because it is how you check your work without counting
everything.

THE PATTERN

Look at the top of the dome. There is a ring of five triangles around the
apex, and every edge of every one of them is an A. Those are the AAA
triangles. There are ten of them in the hemisphere.

Everything else is a BAB triangle: one A and two Bs. There are thirty of
those.

Ten plus thirty is forty triangles, which is the whole dome.

So: if you are looking at a triangle and all three sticks are the same length,
you are near the top. If two are short and one is long, you are not. That is a
check you can do from the ground with your eyes.

WHY THE FAMILIES MATTER MORE IN THIS METHOD

In a normal strut-and-hub dome the families are just two lengths. You cut
sixty of each, you keep them in two piles, and the difference between them is
eight inches.

In the wedge method they are more than that, because the two families sit at
different angles to each other and their seams fold by different amounts.

On the reference build:

* an A seam folds 18.029 degrees
* a B seam folds 22.459 degrees

Same dome, same wedge, four and a half degrees of difference depending on
which family you are looking at. That difference is not an error and it does
not average out. It is the geometry telling you that an A seam and a B seam
are different joints.

Mix up an A and a B and you will not just have a stick of the wrong length.
You will have a stick that wants to sit at the wrong angle.

Keep the piles apart. Mark them before they leave the saw.

sections.title: Triangle types
sections.body:
There are two kinds of triangle in a 2V hemisphere and you can tell them apart
across the room.

AAA TRIANGLES

Three A members. All three sides 72.000 inches. Equilateral -- genuinely
equilateral, not approximately.

There are ten of them, and they live at the top of the dome, in and around the
ring at the apex.

These are the easy ones. Every side is the same, every corner is sixty
degrees, and if one of them comes out wrong you will see it immediately
because it will not be symmetrical.

BAB TRIANGLES

One A and two Bs. Two sides of 63.670 inches and one of 72.000.

There are thirty of them, and they make up everything below the top: the
middle band, the base ring, and every triangle that touches the ground.

These are isosceles, not equilateral. They have a long edge and two short
ones, and the long edge always points the same way relative to the dome --
which is the thing to check when you are assembling, because a BAB fitted
upside down looks nearly right and is not.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR PANELS

If you are building panel by panel -- and in the wedge method you are -- you
are building exactly two kinds of panel.

Ten of one. Thirty of the other.

That is a much better position than it sounds. It means one jig setting for
the AAA panels and one for the BAB panels, and it means the fortieth panel is
the same job as the first.

It also means your total perimeter of panel edge is two numbers rather than
forty. On the reference build an AAA triangle has 216.00 inches of perimeter
and a BAB has 199.34 inches. Ten of the first and thirty of the second is
every edge in the building, and you will want that number when you buy gasket,
tape, or anything else sold by the foot.

THE COUNT, IN ONE PLACE

* 40 triangles
* 10 AAA, 30 BAB
* 26 vertices
* 65 geodesic edges
* 55 of those edges are interior seams, where two triangles meet
* 10 are the base ring, where nothing meets them

Those numbers do not change with size. A nineteen-foot 2V hemisphere and a
forty-foot one have exactly the same counts. Only the lengths move.

sections.title: Triangle heights
sections.body:
The height of a triangle -- the perpendicular distance from one side to the
opposite corner -- is the number that decides whether your panel fits on a
sheet of anything.

It is also the number nobody calculates until they are standing in the
plywood aisle.

THE NUMBERS

On the reference build:

* an AAA triangle is 72.000 inches on every side, and its height is 62.354
  inches
* a BAB triangle has a 72.000 inch long edge and two 63.670 inch sides, and
  its height above the long edge is 52.520 inches

Both of those are the *minimum* width the triangle can be squeezed into. You
cannot rotate a triangle to make it narrower than its shortest altitude.

WHY THAT NUMBER RUINED A PLAN

A sheet of plywood is 48 inches wide.

62.354 is not 48. 52.520 is not 48 either.

No panel of this dome fits on a four-foot sheet. Not in any rotation, not with
any clever nesting, not if you turn it diagonally. The narrowest panel in the
building is still four and a half inches wider than the widest sheet you can
buy at a normal yard.

That is not a small inconvenience. It decides how the whole skin gets built.
You either buy oversized sheet goods, or you sheet across the frame and cut on
site, or you build the panels up from narrower boards.

The reference build sheets across the frame and tapes the joints, because that
is the option that does not require a special order.

CHECK THIS BEFORE YOU DESIGN ANYTHING

Take your longest member. Multiply by 0.866 for an equilateral panel -- that
is your AAA height. Compare it to whatever you were planning to skin the dome
with.

If the answer is bigger than your sheet, you have just found out something
important, and you have found it out for free rather than in a car park with a
sheet of ply that does not fit in the car.

sections.title: Dihedral relationships
sections.body:
This is the section the rest of the book leans on, so it is worth reading
slowly.

A dihedral angle is the angle between two flat faces that share an edge. Open
a book halfway and the angle between the two covers is a dihedral angle.

On a dome, every interior seam is a dihedral. Two triangles meet along a line
and they are not coplanar -- they fold, because that folding is what makes the
flat triangles approximate a curved sphere.

HOW MUCH THEY FOLD

On the reference build:

* an A seam folds 18.029 degrees
* a B seam folds 22.459 degrees

That is the angle the two panels turn through, relative to each other, at
their shared edge.

Fifty-five interior seams in the hemisphere: twenty-five A and thirty B. The
other ten edges are the base ring and they do not fold, because there is
nothing on the other side of them.

WHY A WEDGE METHOD CARES MORE THAN A STRUT METHOD

In a strut-and-hub dome the dihedral is handled at the hub. The hub is a
casting or a plate with the angles built into it, and the struts just arrive.

In the wedge method there is no hub. The dihedral has to be handled by the
timber, and it is handled by the fact that a wedge is wider on one face than
the other.

That is the entire mechanism. A wedge, seen end-on, is a sector of a log -- a
triangle in section. Put two of them side by side along a seam and the
difference in width between their inner and outer faces makes the two panels
turn relative to each other. The wood does the folding.

THE NUMBER THAT MAKES THIS WORK

Split a log into eight, and each sector is 45 degrees.

Now look at what the dome asks for:

* A seam: folds 18.029 degrees, leaves 26.971 degrees
* B seam: folds 22.459 degrees, leaves 22.541 degrees

Add each pair. Both come to exactly 45.

That is not a coincidence and it is not tuned. The raw 45-degree sector is
being split between the fold the dome needs and the gap left over, and the two
always add to the sector angle because that is what a sector is.

WHAT THE LEFTOVER IS

The leftover -- 26.971 degrees on an A seam, 22.541 on a B -- is a gap. Two
sawn faces meeting at a dihedral angle do not close flush. There is a
wedge-shaped void along every one of those fifty-five seams.

Every other way of building a dome treats that as a defect and machines it
out.

This book does not. That gap is the key, it has a chapter of its own, and it
turns out to be the most useful thing in the building.

sections.title: Scaling a design
sections.body:
Scaling a 2V dome is one multiplication, and then a list of things that do not
scale with it.

WHAT SCALES

Pick your new longest member. Divide by 0.618034 to get the radius. Multiply
by 0.546533 to get the B member. Everything geometric follows:

* diameter is twice the radius
* height is the radius, for a hemisphere
* every chord is its factor times the radius

Double the member length and you double the radius, the diameter and the
height.

WHAT SCALES FASTER THAN YOU EXPECT

Area goes as the square. Double the dome and the floor goes up four times, and
so does the skin you have to buy.

The reference build is 19.416 feet across with 277 square feet of decagonal
floor and 592 square feet of spherical envelope. Double it to a member of
twelve feet and the floor is over 1,100 square feet. That is not a bigger
dome; that is a different building with a different budget.

WHAT DOES NOT SCALE AT ALL

The counts. Forty triangles, sixty-five edges, twenty-six vertices, fifty-five
interior seams, 120 members. A nine-foot 2V and a forty-foot 2V have exactly
the same parts list, with different numbers written on it.

The angles. Every dihedral is the same at every size -- 18.029 degrees on an A
seam whether the dome is a playhouse or a hall. Angles are a property of the
shape, not the size, and that is why one jig design works across the whole
range.

WHAT SCALES THE WRONG WAY

Your timber.

The chords scale linearly, but the *stock* you need to cut them from does not
behave as politely. A six-foot member comes out of an eight-foot log with
room. A twelve-foot member does not come out of a sixteen-foot log the same
way, because the taper of a real tree means the wedge cross-section changes
along its length, and the far end of a long member is coming from a thinner
part of the trunk.

There is a size above which you stop being able to get your members out of one
tree, and it arrives sooner than the arithmetic suggests.

THE ADVICE

Scale up by going up in frequency, not by stretching the members.

If you want more span, a 3V dome with the same six-foot sticks covers more
ground than a 2V with nine-foot ones, and every stick still comes off the same
saw, out of the same size log, with the same jig. You get a bigger building
without changing anything about how you make the parts.

Stretching the member is the obvious way to get a bigger dome. Going up a
frequency is the one that keeps the method intact.

chapters.title: 4. Materials
chapters.body:
The method works with bought lumber, with sawn timber from a local mill, and with logs off your own land. It was designed for the third.

The reason is one number. Split a trunk into wedges and you keep about 88 percent of it; mill the same trunk into 2x4s and you keep about 45. Squaring a round log means throwing the round part away, and this method does not square anything.

sections.title: Dimensional lumber
sections.body:
You can build this dome out of bought lumber. It works, it is faster, and it
costs more.

WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE METHOD

A 2x6 is not a wedge. It is the same width on both faces, so it does not do
the thing the method depends on -- the changing width that lets neighbouring
triangles turn relative to each other.

So if you build from dimensional lumber you have two choices.

Rip the wedge yourself. Take a 2x6 and rip it at an angle so one face is
narrower than the other. You now have a wedge with the profile the geometry
wants, and you have thrown away the offcut.

Or give up the wedge and handle the dihedral at the joint instead, with
shims, bevels or plates. That is no longer the wedge method; it is a
conventional dome built out of conventional lumber, and there are better books
about that.

THE COST

At the time of writing, a 2x6x12 at a big-box store is about fourteen dollars,
and it rips and crosscuts into four 2x3x6 struts. That is three dollars fifty
a stick.

A shared-strut dome needs 65 of them. This method needs 120.

So the frame is about four hundred and twenty dollars in wood if you buy it,
against roughly two hundred and thirty for the same dome built the
conventional way.

That is the honest number and it is not enormous either way. Wood is not what
makes a dome expensive.

WHEN BOUGHT LUMBER IS THE RIGHT ANSWER

When you do not have trees. When you are in a hurry. When the dome is small
and the difference is forty dollars. When you want to build one to learn the
method before you commit a woodlot to it.

There is no purity requirement here. The method works with a bought wedge; it
just does not get the thing that makes it interesting.

sections.title: Sawn timber
sections.body:
Sawn timber -- squared stock from a local mill rather than a big-box store --
sits between dimensional lumber and logs, and for a lot of people it is the
practical middle.

WHAT YOU GET

Bigger sections than a lumber yard carries. Rough sawn rather than planed,
which means the stated size is the actual size, not the dressed size.

Usually green, or air-dried rather than kiln-dried.

Usually local species, which may or may not be what the span tables assume.

And usually cheaper per board foot than dressed lumber, sometimes
substantially.

WHY IT SUITS THIS METHOD

A rough-sawn 6x6 or 8x8 rips into wedges very conveniently, and a mill will
often sell you the slabwood and offcuts that a dressed-lumber supplier does
not have.

The dimensional stability is worse than kiln-dried and that matters less here
than it would in a stud wall. The frame is triangulated and the joints are
compression joints; a member that moves a sixteenth is not a problem.

WHAT TO ASK THE MILL

Moisture content, or at least when it was cut.

Whether they will cut to a given section rather than a standard one. Most
small mills will, and having your wedge profile cut at the mill removes the
hardest operation from your shop.

Whether they have anything that has been sitting. Timber that has been in the
stack for a year is drier and cheaper than fresh, and a mill usually has some.

THE OPTION MOST PEOPLE MISS

Ask them to rip the wedges.

A mill has a big enough saw to split a log into eight accurately in a fraction
of the time it takes you, and they charge by the hour. For the price of a
morning of mill time you can skip the entire splitting chapter.

That is not cheating. The method is about what the wedge does in the building,
not about who cut it.

sections.title: Logs
sections.body:
This is what the method is really for.

A log is not a worse version of lumber. It is a different material with a
different economics, and the wedge method exists because squaring it is
wasteful.

THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS

Split a trunk into wedges and you keep about 88 percent of it -- 391 board
feet out of a tree that has 442.

Mill the same trunk into 2x4s and you keep about 45 percent. Two hundred
board feet.

Nearly twice the building, out of the same tree.

That is the whole argument, and it is not subtle. Squaring a round log means
throwing the round part away. The wedge method does not square anything.

WHY IT WORKS OUT THAT WAY

A rectangle inscribed in a circle leaves four corners of waste. Do it once per
board and the waste adds up to more than half the log.

A sector of a circle wastes only the saw kerf. Eight sectors out of a round
log is eight sectors, minus eight thin cuts.

WHAT A LOG COSTS

If it is standing on your land, it costs your time.

If you are buying, a log is sold by the ton or by the board foot and is
substantially cheaper than sawn timber, because you are buying it before
anybody has done anything to it.

THE CATCH, AND IT IS A REAL ONE

Green logs are heavy, they are awkward, and they will do things sawn timber
does not.

They move as they dry. They can have tension in them that makes a rip cut
close on the blade. They have bark, which holds water and insects. They are
never quite straight and never quite round.

The chapter on turning timber into wedges is longer than it would be for
lumber for exactly these reasons.

WHAT THE REFERENCE BUILD ASSUMES

A trunk about twelve inches across, split into eight, yielding sectors that
give a member roughly four and a half inches wide and six inches deep.

Roughly one and a half trees for the whole frame.

Twelve inches is not arbitrary: it is what gives a sector of the right size
for a six-foot member on this dome. A smaller trunk gives a thinner wall and a
bigger one gives you wood to trim off.

sections.title: Species
sections.body:
The method does not care much which tree. The building does.

WHAT MATTERS, IN ORDER

Splitting behaviour. Some species split cleanly and predictably along the
grain; some tear, wander, or spiral. This is the property that decides whether
the method is pleasant or miserable, and it is not on any span table.

Rot resistance, if any part of the frame is near the ground or exposed.

Strength, which matters less than people expect, because a triangulated dome
does not load its members heavily.

Weight, which matters when you are carrying 120 of them.

WHAT SPLITS WELL

Straight-grained softwoods. Pine, spruce, fir, cedar. These are the species the
method was developed around and they split predictably with a froe or on a
saw.

WHAT DOES NOT

Anything with interlocked or spiral grain. Elm is famously difficult. Some
eucalyptus. Any tree that grew on a windy slope and twisted as it went.

You can tell a lot by looking at the bark: if the bark runs in a spiral up the
trunk, the grain does too, and your sectors will come out twisted.

THE ROT QUESTION

Cedar, larch, black locust and osage orange are durable. Pine and spruce are
not.

For a frame that is off the ground, dry, and inside an envelope, durability
barely matters -- the reference build uses pine and expects it to last as long
as the roof over it.

For anything in contact with the ground or outside the envelope, use a durable
species or do not use wood.

THE ADVICE

Use what is growing where you are.

A local species you can get for free and can split reliably beats an ideal
species you have to buy and transport. The method is tolerant, and the frame
is not the part of this building that will fail.

sections.title: Moisture
sections.body:
Green wood is wet wood, and it will get drier after you build with it.

That is not a reason to avoid it. It is a reason to know what it will do.

WHAT HAPPENS AS IT DRIES

Wood shrinks across the grain and barely at all along it.

For a member, that means it gets narrower and shallower and does not get
shorter. Chord lengths stay put. Cross-sections do not.

So a joint that was tight when built gets slightly loose after a season. That
is the single most predictable thing about building with green timber and it
has one answer: come back and tighten everything after the first summer.

HOW MUCH

Softwood shrinks roughly four to eight percent across the grain going from
green to dry, depending on species and direction.

On a member six inches deep that is a quarter to a half inch. Not nothing.

BUILDING GREEN ANYWAY

People have built with green timber for a very long time and the technique is
well understood: use joints that can be tightened, expect to tighten them, and
do not build anything that depends on a dimension staying exactly put.

The pinwheel joint is well suited to this. It is a compression joint held
closed by a fastener, and tightening the fastener takes up the shrinkage.

A joint relying on a precise fit -- a mortice, a dovetail, a machined key --
is not well suited, and that is worth remembering when you are tempted to get
clever at a seam.

WHAT NOT TO DO

Do not seal green timber. Paint, varnish or a tight plastic wrap on wet wood
traps the moisture and you get rot instead of drying.

Do not build it into an unventilated cavity while wet.

Do not assume it is dry because the outside feels dry. A six-inch member is
wet in the middle for a long time.

THE SCHEDULE THAT WORKS

Split green, because green splits far more easily than dry.

Then sticker the sectors -- stacked with spacers, under cover, with air all
round -- for as long as you can stand. Three months makes a real difference.
Six is better.

Then cut to final size, because a member cut dry stays the size you cut it.

sections.title: Knots and defects
sections.body:
Every real tree has defects. The question is which ones matter and where.

KNOTS

A knot is where a branch was. The grain flows round it, which makes the wood
locally stronger in some directions and much weaker in others.

For this method the important thing about a knot is not strength. It is that
knots ruin splits.

A split runs along the grain, and grain goes round a knot. Hit a knot while
splitting and the split wanders, forks or stops.

So: look at the log before you split it, mark the knot clusters, and buck the
log so the clear lengths become members and the knotty lengths become
something else.

WHERE A KNOT IS ACCEPTABLE

In the middle of a member's length, away from the ends, where the member is in
compression and nothing is fastened.

WHERE IT IS NOT

Near an end. Every member gets fastened near both ends, and a fastener into or
beside a knot splits the wood or gets no grip.

On a sawn face that becomes a seam. The seam faces have to be flat and
predictable and a knot there is a lump.

OTHER DEFECTS

Shake -- a separation along the growth rings. A member with shake through it
can come apart along that plane. Reject it.

Check -- surface cracks from drying. Usually cosmetic on a member this size.
Fine.

Sweep -- a gentle bend along the log. Members are short; a six-foot length out
of a long gentle sweep is nearly straight. Usable.

Spiral grain -- the whole log twisted. Splits come out twisted and members
wind. This is the worst defect for this method and it is worth rejecting the
log.

THE RULE

Defects are not a reason to reject wood. They are a reason to decide what each
piece becomes.

The clear butt log becomes A members. The knotty top becomes B members and
blocking. The bad piece becomes jig stock. Almost nothing is actually waste,
which is another part of why the method suits trees you cut yourself.

sections.title: Grain direction
sections.body:
Wood is much stronger along the grain than across it, and every decision in
this chapter follows from that.

IN A MEMBER

The grain runs along the length. That is automatic when you split, because the
split follows the grain -- which is one of the quiet advantages of splitting
over sawing.

A sawn board can have grain running out the side of it, where the saw cut
across a curving grain line. That board is weak and it will break where the
grain runs out. A split member cannot have that, because the split went where
the grain went.

That is worth saying plainly: a split member is stronger for its size than a
sawn one, because splitting cannot cut across the fibres and sawing can.

AT A JOINT

The butting end presents end grain. The receiving face presents side grain.

Compression on end grain is fine -- wood is very strong that way. Compression
on side grain is weaker but adequate at these loads, and the contact area is
large.

A fastener into end grain holds poorly. A fastener into side grain holds well.

So: wherever possible, drive fasteners into the side of a member rather than
into its end. The pinwheel joint arranges this naturally, which is another of
its quiet advantages.

SPLITTING NEAR AN END

The end of a member is where the grain is free to separate, and it is where
every fastener goes.

Pilot every hole. In green timber, near an end, without a pilot, you will
split the piece -- reliably, not occasionally.

THE ORIENTATION QUESTION

A wedge has a curved bark face, two sawn faces, and a point. Which way it goes
in the wall is a real decision and it has its own section in the geometry
chapter.

For grain purposes it does not matter much: the fibres run along the member
whichever way you rotate it. What changes is which face takes the fastener and
which face meets the seam, and those are covered where the geometry is.

sections.title: Fasteners
sections.body:
The frame has 120 joints and every one of them needs fasteners that will still
be doing their job in twenty years.

WHAT THE FASTENERS ACTUALLY DO

They do not hold the dome up. The wood does that, in compression, through the
butt faces.

The fasteners hold the joint closed so the wood can work. That is a smaller
job than it sounds and it changes what you need.

CORROSION

This is the one that decides longevity.

Green timber is wet and many species are acidic. Plain steel in wet acidic
wood corrodes, and corroding steel stains the wood black around it and loses
section.

Use stainless, or a properly coated exterior screw. Not zinc-plated indoor
screws, which will be rust within a couple of damp seasons.

Stainless is expensive at 120 joints and it is the right expense. Work out what
it costs to replace every fastener in a standing dome and the premium stops
looking large.

QUANTITY

Two or three per joint, 120 joints, so somewhere between 240 and 360
structural fasteners for the frame.

Plus pilot holes for every one of them.

THE INSERT OPTION

A threaded insert set into the receiving member, with a bolt threading into
it, gives a joint you can undo and remake indefinitely because the thread
lives in metal rather than wood.

Two per joint is 240 inserts. It is more money and more work at build time and
it is the difference between a dome you can take apart once and a dome you can
take apart repeatedly.

BUY FOR THE DOME AFTER NEXT

If there is any chance you will build a bigger one, buy the bolts long now.

A bolt cut about a third longer than this dome needs still reaches through the
thicker members of the next two sizes up. The extra length costs pennies and
saves re-buying every fastener in the building.

sections.title: Plates and reinforcement
sections.body:
The short version: you do not need them, and here is when you might want them
anyway.

WHY THE FRAME DOES NOT NEED THEM

The pinwheel joint is a compression joint. Wood pressed against wood, with a
large contact area, at loads well within what softwood takes across the grain.

A steel plate does not improve that. The wood is already carrying it.

Plates and brackets exist in other dome systems because those systems put
their joints in tension and shear, where wood is weak and steel is not. This
one does not.

WHERE REINFORCEMENT IS ACTUALLY WORTH IT

Three places.

The base connection. Uplift is the load case that matters on a dome -- it is a
very good aerofoil and it is light. Every base vertex wants a strap or an
anchor holding it down, and that is a tension connection where steel belongs.

Around openings. Cutting a door or window out of a triangulated shell
interrupts the triangulation. The members either side of the hole are carrying
what the missing ones used to, and they may want help.

Point loads. A hoist, a heavy fixture, a partition carrying something. The
frame takes those locally if you give it something to take them with.

WHAT TO AVOID

Plating every joint "to be safe".

That is not safer. It adds cost, adds thermal bridges through the envelope,
adds visible steel to an interior that is mostly visible, and -- the part that
matters -- it hides whether the joints are working.

If the frame needs plates everywhere, something is wrong with the joints and
the plates are covering it up rather than fixing it.

THE HONEST LIMIT OF THIS CHAPTER

Nothing here is an engineering specification.

Species, moisture, snow load, wind exposure and local code all change the
answer, and no book can know yours. What this chapter can tell you is what the
joint is -- a butt in compression, fasteners holding it closed -- and that is
the description an engineer needs to size it for your site.

If the dome is a workshop, build it as described and sleep fine. If people are
going to live in it, take this description to somebody who can stamp it.

chapters.title: 5. Turning Timber Into Wedges
chapters.body:
This is the chapter where a tree becomes a building material, and it is the one that has no equivalent in a normal dome book.

A strut-and-hub builder buys lumber. Here you are making the lumber, and the shape you make it into is what carries the dome's geometry. Get this chapter right and the assembly is straightforward. Get it wrong and no amount of care later will recover it.
chapters.notes:
CHAPTER GOAL: Build a practical, illustrated chapter covering 5. Turning Timber Into Wedges.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Layout
sections.body:
Layout is deciding, before any saw runs, which part of the tree becomes which
part of the building.

Do it badly and you will run out of good wood halfway through and start using
the parts you set aside for a reason.

START AT THE BUTT

The bottom of the trunk is the best wood in the tree. Straightest grain,
fewest knots, largest diameter.

Your longest members should come from there. On the reference build that is
the sixty A members at six feet each.

The top of the trunk is smaller, knottier, and tapers faster. That is where
the short members and the offcuts come from.

This sounds obvious. It is routinely got wrong, because people buck the log
into equal lengths first and then decide what each piece is for -- by which
point the decision has already been made for them.

Decide first. Then cut.

HOW MUCH TREE

The reference build needs about one and a half trees of usable stock for 120
members: 664 feet of member at a six-inch depth and four and a half inch
average width.

"One and a half trees" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. It assumes a
trunk you can get six-foot clear lengths out of, straight enough to split
predictably, and about twelve inches across.

A twelve-inch trunk split into eight gives sectors that are the right size for
this dome. A smaller trunk gives you smaller sectors and a thinner wall. A
bigger one gives you sectors you will have to trim, which is wasted work and
wasted wood.

MARK BEFORE YOU BUCK

Chalk the whole log while it is still one piece.

Mark where each member will come from, mark the direction of the taper, and
mark anything you are avoiding -- a knot cluster, a bend, a shake.

Once the log is in pieces you have lost the information about which end was
up, and which end was up matters for the taper.

THE ONE THAT CATCHES EVERYONE

A tree is not a cylinder. It is a cone.

A six-foot length taken from a twelve-inch butt is twelve inches at one end
and perhaps eleven at the other. Split that into eight and every sector is
wider at one end than the other.

You cannot avoid that. You can only decide which end of the member the fat end
goes, and be consistent about it across all 120 pieces. Pick a rule now --
fat end toward the vertex, say -- and write it on the wall.

sections.title: Ripping
sections.body:
Ripping is cutting along the grain. Everything that turns a log into a wedge
is a rip.

THE DIFFERENCE THAT MATTERS

A crosscut goes across the fibres and is over quickly. A rip goes along them,
and the fibres want to steer the blade.

That means rips wander. A rip that starts true can finish an eighth of an inch
off, and in green timber with tension in it, more.

Everything in this chapter is a way of fighting that.

BLADE

Use a rip blade -- fewer teeth, bigger gullets, aggressive hook. A crosscut
blade will do it and will burn, bind and wander.

Sharp matters more than anything else. A dull blade in a rip cut is how
kickback happens, and green softwood dulls a blade faster than dry hardwood
because of the resin.

FEED RATE

Slower than feels right at first, then steady.

The mistake is varying the feed. A rip cut that speeds up and slows down
produces a wandering line, because the blade deflects differently under
different load. Pick a rate you can hold for the whole cut and hold it.

TENSION

Green logs have internal stress. As you cut into one it can close on the
blade, or spring open, and both are dangerous.

Use a riving knife or a wedge in the kerf behind the blade. Always. Not for
the first few cuts until you see how the log behaves -- from the first cut,
because the one that closes is the one you did not expect.

If a cut starts to pinch, stop, back out, and wedge it open before continuing.

THE ORDER

Cut the log in half first, then quarters, then eighths.

Halving a round log is the hardest cut because there is no flat face to
reference. Once you have a flat, every subsequent cut has something to sit on,
and the whole job gets easier as it goes.

sections.title: Log division
sections.body:
Splitting a log into eight is the operation the whole method rests on.

Eight sectors of 45 degrees each. Those 45 degrees are what the dome's
dihedral angles come out of, which is covered in the geometry chapter and is
worth reading before you cut.

WHY EIGHT

Not because the geometry demands it.

Eight is what a person can do accurately. Halving is easy -- you find the
centre and cut through it. Halving again is easy. Halving a third time gives
you eight, and each cut references a flat face that already exists.

Six or twelve means cutting angles that are not repeated halvings, and that
means measuring rather than referencing.

The reference build uses eight because of that, not because 45 degrees is
special. If you can hold twelve accurately, twelve works and gives you thinner
sticks.

FINDING THE CENTRE

Not the centre of the bark. The centre of the wood.

A tree is not round and the pith is not in the middle. Find the pith at both
ends, mark it, and run your first cut through both marks. That is the cut that
makes the other seven work.

Get this one wrong and every sector is a different size, and you will not find
out until you are assembling.

THE SEQUENCE

* find the pith at both ends, mark it
* cut through both marks: two halves
* each half, cut through the pith again: four quarters
* each quarter, cut through the pith again: eight sectors

Every cut after the first has a flat face to run against a fence, which is why
this gets easier rather than harder.

WHAT YOU GET

Eight sectors, each a 45-degree wedge in cross-section, each with two sawn
faces meeting at the pith and one curved bark face on the outside.

The sawn faces are the ones that matter. They are what meets the neighbouring
member at a seam, and the angle between them is the 45 degrees the geometry
uses.

The bark face is the outside of the dome. Leave it or take it off -- the
method does not care structurally, but bark holds moisture and insects, so
most people take it off.

sections.title: Wedge extraction
sections.body:
Extraction is getting a usable member out of a sector.

The sector is 45 degrees of a tapering cone. The member needs to be a
consistent cross-section over its length. Those are not the same thing, and
the difference is the work.

THE TAPER PROBLEM

A sector from a log that is twelve inches at the butt and eleven at the top is
wider at one end.

For a six-foot member that difference is about half an inch across the width.
Small enough to live with in a frame; too big to ignore when you are trying to
make forty identical panels.

Two ways to handle it.

TRIM TO THE SMALL END

Take every sector down to the cross-section of its narrow end.

Consistent members, predictable panels, and you throw away the difference.
Simplest and most wasteful.

USE IT ORIENTED

Keep the taper and decide, once, which way it faces.

Every member has its fat end toward the vertex, say, and its thin end toward
the middle of the edge. Every panel is then identically tapered and the panels
still match each other, because they are all wrong in the same direction.

More wood kept, more discipline required, and completely dependent on doing it
the same way 120 times.

The reference build trims to the small end, because the first dome is not the
place to be clever. Once you have built one, the oriented method is worth the
saving.

WHAT COMES OFF

The head end. Where the member meets a vertex, material has to come off to
make room for the joint.

That offcut is not scrap -- it is the right size for blocking, for the jig
itself, and for the keys that fill the seams. Keep a box of it.

THE RULE

Extract every member the same way, in the same order, referencing the same
faces.

A sector is an irregular object and there are four different ways to set it on
a bench. Three of them are wrong for your cut and all four look reasonable.
Mark the reference face on every sector as it comes off the splitting station
and always put that face down.

sections.title: Saw setups
sections.body:
A setup is a saw, a fence, a stop and a blade height, held constant while you
run a batch through it.

The number of setups in this build is small. The number of *cuts* is large.
That ratio is the thing to protect.

THE SETUPS YOU NEED

Splitting: a rip setup with a tall fence and a riving knife.

Length: a crosscut setup with a stop block, one for A members and one for B.

Butting ends: an angled crosscut, referenced off a fence at the butt angle.

Receiving faces: a shallow cut along the side of the member, referenced off
the same fence.

That is four setups for 120 members and about 300 cuts.

CHANGE THE SETUP AS SELDOM AS POSSIBLE

Every setup change is an opportunity for the new setting to be slightly
different from the old one.

If you do all sixty A lengths, then change to B, then change back because you
miscounted, the second batch of A members is not guaranteed to match the
first.

Do all of an operation. Count before you change. Then change once.

THE STOP BLOCK

A stop block sets length without measuring, which is the single biggest
accuracy win available.

Clamp it, cut one, check it, then cut the rest without measuring anything.

Check it again every tenth piece. Stop blocks creep -- the clamp relaxes, the
block gets knocked, sawdust builds up behind it. Ten pieces is often enough to
catch creep while it is still small.

AND THE THING THAT WILL BITE YOU

Sawdust behind the stop.

A sixteenth of packed dust between the workpiece and the stop makes every
subsequent piece a sixteenth long, and it accumulates invisibly over a batch.

Blow it out between pieces. Every piece. It takes a second and it removes an
entire category of error.

sections.title: Jigs
sections.body:
A jig is a fixture that holds a workpiece in a known position so a cut lands
in the right place without being measured.

In this method, the jig is the method. One flat jig turns 120 irregular
split-log sectors into forty identical panels, and without it the whole
approach falls apart.

WHAT IT DOES

It holds three members in the relationship they will have in a finished
triangle, and presents each joint to the saw at the right angle.

You do not measure the joint. You put the stick against the fences, and the
joint comes out right because the fences are in the right places.

WHY THAT MATTERS SO MUCH HERE

The members are not rectangular. They are wedges, with a curved face and two
sawn faces at 45 degrees, and no two are exactly alike because they came out
of a real tree.

You cannot reference an irregular object off itself. You have to reference it
off something known, and the jig is that something.

THE FENCES

The jig in the tool has coloured fences and they do different jobs:

* the rail sets the stick's point-axis across the panel
* the red fence is the sawn face that must land on the seam side
* the green fence is the sawn face the next butt lands on
* the magenta plate is the head-end flush-cut fence
* the cyan plate is the receiving face the next member's butt meets
* the clamp holds the stick down on rail and fences

Six references, and every one of them is a physical stop rather than a number.

BUILD THE JIG FIRST

Before any member is cut to final size.

The jig is made out of offcut from the splitting, so it costs nothing but
time, and it is the thing every other operation depends on. A jig that is a
degree out makes 120 members a degree out.

Build it, check it, and check it against the tool's own drawings rather than
against your expectations.

THE TEST

Make one panel. If all three corners close and the triangle sits flat on the
floor, the jig is right.

If they do not, the jig is wrong, and it is wrong now -- before it has made
119 more.

sections.title: Repetitive cutting
sections.body:
The forty-first identical cut is where accuracy goes to die.

Not because the saw changed. Because you did.

WHAT ACTUALLY DEGRADES

Attention first. By the thirtieth piece you are no longer checking that the
stick is against the fence; you are assuming it is.

Then technique. You get faster, and faster means less pressure on the fence,
and less pressure means the piece can lift.

Then the setup, slowly, from vibration and sawdust and the clamp relaxing.

None of those announce themselves.

THE COUNTERMEASURES

Work in batches of ten, not sixty. After each ten, check one against the
master, blow out the stop, and take thirty seconds.

That is not a break for you. It is a checkpoint for the work, and it caps how
many pieces a drifting setup can ruin at ten.

Count out loud or make a mark. You will lose count otherwise, and a batch of
nine or eleven is how the A and B counts end up uneven.

Stop when you are tired. The last hour of a long session produces most of the
errors, and a piece cut wrong at eight in the evening costs more than the hour
you would have saved.

THE THING THAT HELPS MOST

Do not think of it as 120 cuts.

Think of it as twelve batches of ten, each with a check at the end. Twelve is
a number you can hold. 120 is a number you stop counting.

That is a psychological trick and it works, which is the only test that
matters.

sections.title: Tolerances
sections.body:
A tolerance is how wrong a part is allowed to be before it stops working.

Stating them is worth doing because without a stated tolerance every part is
either perfect or scrap, and neither is true.

WHAT THIS BUILD CAN LIVE WITH

Member length: plus or minus a sixteenth of an inch. The joints take up under
the fastener and a sixteenth vanishes.

End angles: within half a degree. This is the tight one. An angle error does
not take up -- it holds the joint open and it accumulates round a ring.

Cross-section: a quarter inch of variation is fine. The members are split from
real trees and they are not going to be identical. The frame does not care.

Panel flatness: a triangle that rocks by more than a sixteenth on a flat floor
is telling you an end angle is out.

WHY ANGLE IS TIGHTER THAN LENGTH

Because length errors are random and angle errors are systematic.

If your stop block is right and your technique is variable, lengths scatter
either side of the target and they cancel around the dome.

If your fence is set half a degree off, every single angle is off by the same
half degree in the same direction, and ten of them round a base ring is five
degrees of accumulated error with nowhere to go.

Length errors average out. Angle errors add up. That is the whole reason for
the different tolerance.

MEASURE THE RIGHT THING

Do not measure a member's length with a tape against the curved bark face.

Measure between the reference faces -- the sawn faces the jig uses. Those are
the surfaces the geometry actually uses, and the bark face is decoration.

WHEN TO SCRAP A PIECE

If it is long, it is not scrap. Recut it.

If it is short, it may still be a B member, or blocking, or jig stock.

If the angle is wrong, recut the end. If both ends are wrong, it is blocking.

Very little of this actually becomes waste, which is the compensation for
using eighty percent more wood than a shared-strut dome.

sections.title: Labeling
sections.body:
Label everything, as it is made, with something that survives.

This is the least interesting section in the book and skipping it will cost
you a day.

WHAT NEEDS A LABEL

Every member: which family it is, A or B.

Every member: which face is the receiving face. This is not visible once the
stick is out of the jig, and fitting a member with its receiving face on the
wrong side mirrors the panel.

Every panel: which triangle it is, AAA or BAB, and which way is up. A BAB
panel fitted upside down looks nearly right.

Every sector, before it becomes a member: which face is the reference face,
and which end was the butt of the tree.

HOW TO MARK

One line for A, two lines for B. Not the letters -- they look alike upside
down in bad light at the bottom of a pile, and you will be reading them from
across the shop.

Use a lumber crayon or a keel, not pencil. Pencil disappears off rough sawn
timber the first time it rains or gets handled.

Mark on the end grain where possible. It is the part you see when the stick is
in a stack.

WHEN TO MARK

As the piece comes off the saw. Not at the end of the batch.

"I will know which pile is which" is true for about four minutes.

THE PANEL LABEL

Once a panel is assembled, write its number on it -- and write it on the
inside face, because the outside is going to be covered.

The tool numbers the panels and the fabrication package prints the list. Use
those numbers rather than inventing your own, so that when something does not
fit you can describe it to somebody in terms they can look up.

THE COST OF NOT DOING THIS

A pile of 120 unlabelled split-log members all look broadly similar, and
telling a 72.000 inch chord from a 63.670 inch one by eye is harder than it
sounds when both sticks are tapered, irregular, and lying at an angle.

You will end up measuring all of them. That is the day it costs.

chapters.title: 6. Making the Struts
chapters.body:
Cutting a hundred and twenty sticks is not a hundred and twenty problems. It is about six problems, repeated, and this chapter is the six.

The one worth reading twice is the first. The chord is not the cut, and every dome that has ever been built a hundred and twenty sticks too short was built by somebody who assumed it was.
chapters.notes:
CHAPTER GOAL: Build a practical, illustrated chapter covering 6. Making the Struts.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Cutting length
sections.body:
The chord is not the cut.

This is the single most expensive misunderstanding in dome building and it
catches people who have done everything else right.

The chord is the distance between two vertex points. Those points are
mathematical -- they float in space at the corners of the triangles, and on
the reference build they are 72.000 inches apart for an A member.

The stick you cut is shorter than that, because both of its ends get taken
back to make room for the members it meets.

THE NUMBERS ON THE REFERENCE BUILD

A members: 72.000 inch chord, and the usable stock comes off the saw between
68.977 and 70.182 inches.

B members: 63.670 inch chord, stock between 60.492 and 62.681 inches.

Look at the range. It is not one number. A members are not all the same
length, even though they are all the same chord.

WHY THE RANGE EXISTS

Because the amount taken off an end depends on what that end runs into.

In the pinwheel joint every member butts into the side of its neighbour rather
than meeting it point to point. How far it has to be set back depends on how
thick the neighbour is at that spot and what angle it arrives at. Those are
not the same at every corner of the dome.

So an A member near the apex is trimmed slightly differently from an A member
in the middle band, and the difference is up to an inch and a fifth.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR CUT LIST

You cannot cut sixty identical A members and sixty identical B members and
expect them to go together.

You need the actual per-member list, and the tool generates it. Run the
fabrication package and you get every member with its own length, its own
identifier, and the panel it belongs to.

THE ONE THING TO DO ANYWAY

Cut long.

Every member is easier to shorten than to lengthen, and the first panel you
build is the one that tells you whether your numbers are right. Cut the first
three members half an inch over, fit them, measure what you actually needed,
and then commit the other 117.

Half an inch of sacrificial length on three sticks is the cheapest insurance
in the whole build.
