sections.title: End geometry
sections.body:
What happens at the end of a member is more important than how long the member
is.

A length that is out by a sixteenth makes a slightly loose joint. An end angle
that is out by a degree makes a joint that does not sit down, and a panel that
will not lie flat, and forty panels that will not agree with each other.

WHAT THE END ACTUALLY HAS TO DO

In the pinwheel joint, each member does two different things at its two ends.

At one end it butts into the side of its neighbour. That end needs a flat face
cut square across the stick, at the angle the neighbour presents.

At the other end it receives a butt from a different member. That end needs a
flat face on its side for the neighbour to land on.

So every stick has a butting end and a receiving face, and they are not the
same operation.

THE PART THAT IS EASIER THAN IT SOUNDS

Here is the good news, and it is the reason this method exists.

Every one of those cuts is a plain angle. No compound mitre. No bevel and
mitre at the same time. No holding a workpiece at two angles at once while a
blade comes at it.

You are making flat cuts across a stick at a stated angle, which is the thing
a mitre saw does well and a person can check with a protractor.

That is the trade the wedge method makes. It uses more wood -- eighty percent
more than a dome that shares its struts -- and in return every cut is a cut
you can make accurately at two in the afternoon on your fourth day.

THE FENCES

The jig holds the stick with the cut faces referenced off fences rather than
off measurements.

A fence is a physical stop. You put the stick against it and the cut is right,
or the stick does not fit against it and you know immediately. That is a much
better failure mode than a measurement, which can be wrong quietly.

Every cut in this method should be referenced off a fence. If you find
yourself measuring and marking a cut angle with a bevel gauge, you are doing
it the way the method is trying to save you from.

sections.title: Repeatability
sections.body:
You are making 120 members. The question is not whether you can make one
correctly. It is whether the hundred and twentieth is the same as the first.

WHERE DRIFT COMES FROM

Three places, in order of how much damage they do.

A fence that moves. If the stop that sets your length shifts by a
thirty-second over forty cuts, the last stick is an eighth short and nothing
tells you.

A blade that wanders. A saw with play in the pivot cuts a slightly different
angle depending on how hard you push it.

You. Cut fifty of anything and your technique changes -- you get faster, you
push differently, you stop checking.

WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT

Do not measure from the last piece. Ever.

If you use the stick you just cut to set the length of the next one, every
error is inherited and added to. Forty sticks later you have accumulated forty
small mistakes into one large one. Always measure from the fence, or from a
master.

Keep a master. Cut one member, check it properly, and hang it on the wall. It
is not for building with. It is the thing you compare against every tenth
piece, and it is how you catch a fence that has crept without noticing when it
started.

Check at intervals, not at the end. Every tenth member, put it against the
master. If it matches, you have lost nothing. If it does not, you have nine
bad sticks to redo rather than fifty-nine.

THE HONEST BIT

You will still get some wrong.

The point of all of this is not to make a hundred and twenty perfect members.
It is to make sure that when one is wrong you find out while it is still one.

sections.title: A and B members
sections.body:
Sixty A members and sixty B members. Eight and a third inches of chord between
them.

That difference is big enough to see and small enough to get away from you in
a pile.

KEEP THEM APART FROM THE FIRST CUT

Not after. From the first cut.

Two stacks, two locations, and mark every stick as it comes off the saw. Not
later, not when you have a few. As it comes off.

A pencil mark on the end grain takes one second and survives the whole build.
An unmarked stick in the wrong pile costs you a panel.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN IT SOUNDS

If these were just two lengths, mixing them up would be an annoyance. You
would offer up a stick, find it too short, and reach for another.

But in the wedge method the two families sit at different angles. An A seam
folds 18.029 degrees; a B seam folds 22.459. The member is not just a length,
it is a length at an angle, and a B member fitted where an A belongs is wrong
in a way that partially fits.

That is the dangerous kind of wrong. It goes in. It looks close. The panel
comes out slightly off and you do not know why, and by the time you find it
you have built six more.

THE MARKING SCHEME

Use something you cannot misread at a glance:

* A members get one mark
* B members get two

Not "A" and "B" in pencil, which look similar upside down in poor light at the
bottom of a pile. One line or two lines. You can count that from across the
shop.

Mark the receiving face too, while you are at it, and mark it differently.
Which face receives a butt is not obvious once the stick is out of the jig,
and getting it backwards mirrors the panel.

THE COUNT

Sixty of each. If you have cut sixty-one of one and fifty-nine of the other,
something went in the wrong pile and you want to know now.

Count them before you start assembling. Counting 120 sticks takes two minutes.
Finding the miscount at panel thirty-eight takes an afternoon.

sections.title: Test fitting
sections.body:
Build one panel before you cut a hundred and twenty members.

That is the whole section. Everything below is why.

WHAT THE FIRST PANEL TELLS YOU

Three members, three joints, one triangle. It takes an hour and it checks
every assumption you have made:

* whether your cut lengths are right
* whether your end angles are right
* whether the jig holds what you thought it held
* whether the wedge orientation you chose does what you expected
* whether the joint pulls up tight or leaves a gap

Any one of those being wrong is a thing you want to find out on three sticks
rather than on a hundred and twenty.

HOW TO CHECK IT

Lay the finished panel on a flat floor.

It should sit down on all three corners with no rock. If it rocks, one of your
end cuts is off and the triangle is not planar.

Measure the three sides between the vertex points. They should match the
chords for that triangle type -- all 72.000 for an AAA, or 72.000 and two of
63.670 for a BAB.

Measure both diagonals from each corner to the middle of the opposite side.
For an AAA they should be identical. If they are not, your triangle is not
symmetrical and one member is long.

THEN BUILD THE SECOND ONE

The first panel tells you whether you can build a panel. The second tells you
whether you can build the same panel twice.

Put them on top of each other. They should agree everywhere. Any difference
between panel one and panel two is a difference that will be in all forty, and
it is much easier to find now.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE TEST PANELS

Use them. They are real panels and there is nothing wrong with them.

Unless there is, in which case take them apart and find out why, and be
grateful it cost you two panels.

sections.title: Error checking
sections.body:
Errors in a dome do not stay where you put them.

A dome is a closed shape. Every panel has to agree with its neighbours all the
way round, and when you get back to where you started, the last panel either
fits or it does not. There is no slack to absorb a mistake and nowhere to hide
it.

That makes the last panel an extremely good, extremely late test.

FINDING IT EARLIER

Check the sticks. Every tenth member against your master, as described
earlier.

Check the panels. Every panel against the first good one. They should stack.

Check the rings. As you assemble, the base ring should close on itself and sit
level. If the tenth base vertex does not land where the geometry says, stop.
Do not force it. Something upstream is wrong and forcing it will push the
error into the next ring.

THE ERRORS THAT ADD UP AND THE ONES THAT DO NOT

Random errors mostly cancel. If half your sticks are a sixteenth long and half
are a sixteenth short, the dome closes and nobody notices.

Systematic errors do not cancel. If every stick is a sixteenth long because
your fence is a sixteenth out, then by the time you have gone round the base
ring you are ten sixteenths out -- more than half an inch -- and the last
panel will tell you about it.

So the question to ask when something does not fit is not "how big is this
error". It is "is this error in all of them".

Measure three sticks from different points in the run. If all three are long
by the same amount, you have a systematic error and a fence to adjust. If they
disagree randomly, you have a technique problem and a different fix.

WHEN TO STOP AND WHEN TO CARRY ON

Stop if a ring will not close, if a panel rocks, or if the same measurement
comes out differently twice.

Carry on if a joint has a small gap that closes when the fastener pulls up, or
if a member is a sixteenth under. Wood moves, joints take up, and a dome that
is built to a sixteenth is built better than most houses.

The skill is telling those two apart, and it comes from having checked enough
things that you know what normal looks like.

sections.title: Mass-production workflow
sections.body:
Forty panels is a production run, not a project. Treat it like one and it goes
quickly. Treat it like forty separate builds and it does not.

THE ORDER THAT WORKS

Do every operation on every piece before moving to the next operation.

Split all the wedges. Then cut all the A members to rough length. Then all the
Bs. Then do every butting end. Then every receiving face. Then assemble.

This feels slower than building a panel at a time. It is substantially faster,
for three reasons.

You set the jig once per operation instead of forty times. Setup is the
expensive part of any cut; doing it once for sixty sticks rather than once per
panel removes almost all of it.

Your hands learn. The tenth identical operation is faster than the first and
the fiftieth is faster again. That only happens if you do them in a run.

Errors show up in batches. If a fence is wrong you find it on the third stick
of an operation, not on the third panel -- and you have three to redo instead
of a panel to take apart.

THE STATIONS

Set up the shop as stations rather than as a bench.

* the splitting station, where logs become sectors
* the length station, where sectors become members
* the joint station, where members get their ends
* the assembly station, where members become panels
* the stack, where finished panels live

Material moves one way through those. Nothing goes backwards. If you find
yourself carrying a stick back to a previous station, something is wrong with
the sequence and it is worth stopping to fix.

WHERE THE TIME ACTUALLY GOES

Not where you expect.

The cuts are quick. Splitting is quick once you have done a few. What takes
the time is handling -- picking things up, putting them down, finding the one
you want, deciding which pile it goes in.

So the highest-value thing in the whole shop is not a better saw. It is a
place to put things down that keeps them sorted.

Two racks, labelled, within reach of the saw, will save you more hours than
any tool you could buy.

THE REALISTIC SCHEDULE

The reference build assumes roughly 135 hours of labour for the frame,
including splitting the timber.

That is not a weekend. It is three or four solid weeks of evenings, or two
people for a week and a half. Anybody who tells you a dome frame goes up in a
weekend is talking about a kit with the parts already cut.

chapters.title: 7. Connections
chapters.body:
The pinwheel joint carries the building through wood pressed against wood. The fasteners are not holding the dome up. They are holding the joint closed so the wood can.

That distinction runs through this whole chapter, and it is why a method with no hubs and no brackets is not missing anything. It is also why the fastener choices here are mostly about getting the joint apart again rather than about strength.

sections.title: Direct wood joints
sections.body:
The pinwheel joint is wood against wood. No plate, no hub, no bracket.

Three members meet at each corner of a triangle. Instead of all three running
to a single point, each one butts into the side of the next, and they chase
each other round the corner. That is the pinwheel.

WHAT IT BUYS YOU

No end of any member is mitred. Every cut is a plain angle across a stick.

That is the entire reason this method exists, and it is worth being clear
about what it replaces: in a hub dome, the angles live in the hub, and the hub
is either an expensive casting or a piece of steel somebody has to fabricate
accurately. In a hubless dome without the pinwheel, the angles live in
compound mitres cut on the ends of every stick, which is a cut most people
cannot make repeatably.

The pinwheel moves the angle out of the joint and into the *arrangement*. The
sticks are simple; the pattern is clever.

WHAT IT COSTS

Eighty percent more timber.

A dome that shares one strut between two triangles uses 65 members and 369
feet of stock. The pinwheel gives every triangle its own three sticks: 120
members, 664 feet.

That is not a small tax and this book is not going to pretend it is. You are
buying simple cuts with wood.

Whether that is a good trade depends entirely on where your wood comes from.
If you are buying dimensional lumber by the foot, it is an expensive trade. If
you are splitting your own trees, it is close to free, and the chapter on
harvest explains why.

WHERE THE LOAD GOES

Each member is in compression along its length, and it delivers that
compression into the side of its neighbour through a flat face.

Wood is strong in compression across the grain at these loads, and the contact
area is large -- the full width of the member. This is a much better loading
condition than a fastener in shear, which is what most bracket systems rely
on.

The fasteners in a pinwheel joint are not really carrying the building. They
are holding the members against each other so that the wood can do the work.
That distinction matters when you choose them.

sections.title: Screws
sections.body:
Screws are the default fastener for this method and they are the right one for
most of the building.

WHY SCREWS AND NOT NAILS

You can take a screw out.

That is nearly the whole argument. A dome frame is a thing you will adjust,
and the first one you build you will adjust a lot. A nailed joint is a
decision; a screwed joint is a proposal.

Screws also pull. A nail holds two pieces where they are; a screw draws them
together. In a pinwheel joint that matters, because the joint wants the butt
face pressed hard against the receiving face, and a screw does that on its
own.

WHAT NOT TO USE

Drywall screws. They are brittle, they snap under torque, and the head shears
off leaving a stub you cannot get out. They cost almost nothing and they will
cost you an afternoon.

Anything not rated for exterior use, anywhere that will ever be damp.

DRILL THE PILOT

In green timber, near an end, without a pilot hole, you will split the wood.

Not sometimes. Reliably.

Every fastener in a pinwheel joint is going in near the end of a member, which
is the worst place for splitting, and split timber at a joint is a joint that
has already failed. Pilot every one.

That is 120 joints with two or three fasteners each. It is a lot of holes and
it is not optional.

LENGTH

The screw has to pass through the butting member and get well into the
receiving one. On a member six inches deep, that means a long screw -- and it
means the screw is working across most of the joint, which is what you want.

Do not use a fastener that only just makes it. A screw that reaches two
threads into the receiving member is a screw that will pull out when the wood
dries and shrinks.

sections.title: Structural screws
sections.body:
A structural screw is not a longer wood screw. It is a different product with
a published capacity.

WHAT MAKES ONE STRUCTURAL

A stated, tested load rating. That is the difference that matters. A
structural screw comes with a number you can design against; a hardware-store
screw comes with a box.

They also have a hardened shank, a thread designed for withdrawal rather than
just driving, and usually a head that will not cam out under real torque.

Most of them do not need a pilot hole in dimensional lumber. In green
split timber near an end, drill one anyway.

WHERE TO USE THEM

At the pinwheel joints. All 120 of them.

This is the load path of the entire building and it is not the place to save
four pounds. The joints are the only thing holding the dome's shape, and if
one fails the load goes to its neighbours, which are already carrying their
own.

WHERE NOT TO BOTHER

Everywhere else.

Battens, blocking, trim, temporary bracing, panel fixings -- ordinary
exterior-rated screws are fine and considerably cheaper. Using structural
screws for everything is a way of spending money without making the building
better.

THE HONEST LIMIT

This book cannot tell you what size or how many.

That depends on your timber species, your moisture content, your snow load,
your wind exposure and your local code, and anyone who gives you a number
without knowing those is guessing. What this book can tell you is that the
joint is a butt in compression with fasteners holding it closed, and that is
the information an engineer needs to size the fastener for you.

If the dome is a shed, use good structural screws at every joint and sleep
fine. If people are going to live in it, get the fastener schedule stamped.

sections.title: Bolts
sections.body:
A bolt goes all the way through and has a nut on the other side. That is the
difference from a screw, and it changes what the joint can do.

WHEN A BOLT IS BETTER

When you want to take it apart and put it back together more than once.

A screw into wood loses holding power every time you remove and refit it --
the threads cut a slightly bigger hole each time. A bolt does not care. The
bolt bears on the hole and the nut does the clamping, and you can undo it a
hundred times.

That matters for a dome you intend to move, and it matters enormously for the
first dome you build, which you will take apart at least once.

WHEN A BOLT IS WORSE

When you cannot reach the back of it.

Every bolt needs access to both sides. In a finished dome with panels in, a
lot of joints have one accessible side and one buried. A bolt there is a bolt
you cannot ever tighten.

Plan the bolted joints before the panels go on, not after.

THE THREADED INSERT

There is a middle option and it is the one the reference build is heading
toward.

Set a threaded insert into the receiving member -- a metal sleeve with an
internal thread, driven into a drilled hole. Then a bolt from the butting
member threads into that.

The insert takes the thread so the wood never does. You get the repeatability
of a bolt without needing access to the far side, and you can undo and remake
the joint indefinitely without chewing out the hole.

Two per joint, 120 joints, 240 inserts.

BUY THE BOLTS LONG

If you think you might ever build a bigger dome, buy the bolts for the bigger
one now.

A bolt cut thirty-five percent longer than this dome needs will still reach
through the thicker members of the next two sizes up. The extra length costs
pennies per bolt and saves re-buying 240 fasteners later.

That is the cheapest forward decision in the whole build and almost nobody
makes it.

sections.title: Washers
sections.body:
A washer spreads a point load into an area load. In softwood, that is not a
refinement -- it is the difference between a joint that holds and a fastener
that slowly buries itself.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE HERE

Split timber has exposed grain on its sawn faces, and a bolt head bearing
directly on end grain or near-end grain will crush into it under load and
under time.

Once it has crushed in, the joint is loose. Retightening crushes it further.

A wide washer under every bolt head and every nut puts that same load over
several square inches of wood instead of the area of a bolt head.

USE THEM WIDER THAN YOU THINK

The standard washer that comes taped to the bolt is sized for steel.

For timber, go wider. A washer twice the diameter of the standard one costs a
few cents more and quadruples the bearing area.

WHERE THEY GO

Under every nut and under every bolt head. Both ends. Not just the nut side,
which is the side people remember.

BEVELLED WASHERS

If the surface the washer sits on is not square to the bolt -- and on a wedge
it often is not, because the faces are sawn at the sector angle -- a flat
washer bears on one edge only.

A bevelled washer, or a small squared-off pad let into the face, fixes that.
On the reference build most joints are close enough to square that a flat
washer with a large enough diameter is fine. Check yours rather than assuming;
put a washer on and look at whether it sits flat.

THE ONE-SENTENCE VERSION

If you find yourself retightening a bolt more than once, the wood under the
washer has crushed, and a bigger washer would have prevented it.

sections.title: Plates
sections.body:
A plate is a flat piece of metal spanning a joint, fastened to both members.

The wedge method does not need them. This section is about when you might want
them anyway.

WHY THE METHOD DOES NOT NEED THEM

The pinwheel joint carries its load through wood in compression. A plate does
not improve a compression joint -- the wood is already doing the job, and the
plate is along for the ride.

That is the whole point of the method. Hub domes need plates or castings
because their joints are in shear and tension. Pinwheel joints are not.

WHEN TO ADD ONE ANYWAY

Three situations.

Repair. If a member has split at a joint, a plate across it is a reasonable
way to bring it back into service without taking the dome apart.

Uplift. A dome is light and wind gets under it. The base ring joints -- where
the frame meets the floor -- are the ones that see uplift rather than
compression, and those are worth plating or strapping.

Somewhere a load arrives that the geometry did not plan for. A hoist point. A
heavy door frame. A partition carrying a floor above. The frame will take
those loads locally if you give it something to take them with.

WHAT PLATES COST YOU

Visibility. A plate is visible from inside, forever, and a dome interior is
mostly visible.

Thermal bridging, if the plate passes through the insulated envelope.

And a small honesty problem: a dome with plates everywhere is a dome that has
stopped being a wedge dome and started being a bracket dome with wedge-shaped
struts. If you find yourself plating every joint, the method is not working
and the reason is worth finding rather than covering.

sections.title: Internal brackets
sections.body:
An internal bracket sits inside the joint -- between the members, hidden once
assembled.

WHAT THEY ARE FOR

Alignment, mostly. A small internal plate or dowel that locates one member
against another makes assembly faster and stops a joint sliding out of
position while you drive the fastener.

On a 120-joint frame, anything that makes a joint self-locating is worth real
money in time.

THE DOWEL VERSION

The simplest internal bracket is a dowel: a hole in the butting face, a
matching hole in the receiving face, a hardwood pin between them.

The pin does not carry much load. What it does is hold the joint in exactly
one position while you fasten it, which means every joint ends up in the same
place rather than wherever it drifted to.

That is a repeatability tool disguised as a fastener.

THE COST

Every internal bracket is invisible once the dome is together, which sounds
like an advantage and is also a problem: you cannot inspect it.

If an internal bracket corrodes, splits the wood around it, or works loose,
you will find out from the outside -- a joint that has moved -- long after it
started.

So: internal brackets for alignment, external fasteners for load. Then
anything carrying the building can be looked at and tightened without taking
the building apart.

THAT IS THE RULE

Hidden parts should not be load-bearing parts.

Not because hidden parts fail more often. Because when they do, you cannot
tell.

sections.title: External brackets
sections.body:
An external bracket is fastened on the outside of the joint, visible and
reachable.

THE ARGUMENT FOR THEM

You can see them and you can get at them.

Every fastener that carries load should be one you can inspect, tighten and
replace without dismantling anything. An external bracket is the most honest
version of that.

On a building you intend to take apart and move -- which this one is -- that
matters more than on a permanent house. A dome that comes down in a weekend
needs every structural fastener reachable with a driver.

THE ARGUMENT AGAINST

They are on the outside, which means they are in the weather and they are in
the way.

Weather: any bracket outside the envelope needs to be corrosion-rated for the
climate, and the fastener holes through the timber are water paths unless they
are sealed or shielded.

In the way: the outside of the frame is where the skin goes. A bracket
standing proud of the member is a lump the panel has to accommodate, and forty
panels each accommodating three lumps is a lot of fiddling.

THE COMPROMISE THE REFERENCE BUILD MAKES

Fasteners on the inside face, where they are reachable from within the room
and out of the weather entirely.

The inside of a dome is accessible everywhere -- there is no roof space and no
wall cavity. So the inside face is both the sheltered position and the
convenient one, which is unusual and worth taking advantage of.

The outside stays clean for the skin to land on.

sections.title: Temporary assembly joints
sections.body:
A dome does not stand up until it is nearly finished.

Partway through assembly you have a shape that is not yet closed, not yet
stable, and entirely dependent on whatever is propping it. Temporary joints
are how you survive that.

WHAT NEEDS PROPPING

The base ring, until it closes. Ten panels standing on edge in a circle want
to fall inward, and until the tenth one goes in there is nothing stopping
them.

Each subsequent ring, until it closes. Same reason.

The whole dome, until the top ring goes in. A dome without its apex is an arch
with a hole in it, and arches push outward at the base.

THE SIMPLEST RIG

A post in the middle with a temporary platform on it, at the height of each
ring as you build it.

You build the base ring around the post, resting on nothing. You build the
next ring resting on the platform. You raise the platform. Repeat.

That is how domes have been put up by one person for sixty years and there is
no reason to improve on it.

TEMPORARY FASTENERS

Use a screw that comes out easily and a different colour of screw from the
permanent ones.

Different colour matters more than it sounds. At the end of the build you need
to remove every temporary fastener and leave every permanent one, and there
will be several hundred fasteners in the building. If they all look the same
you will either leave temporaries in or take permanents out, and both are bad
in different ways.

THE ORDER TO REMOVE THEM

From the top down, once the dome is closed.

The dome becomes self-supporting when the last panel goes in, not before.
Removing bracing from the bottom while the top is still open takes the props
out from under the thing that is still pushing outward.

sections.title: Replaceable connections
sections.body:
Design every joint on the assumption that somebody will undo it.

This is the section that separates a dome you build from a dome you can live
with for twenty years.

WHY ANYTHING GETS UNDONE

Wood moves. Green timber especially -- it dries, it shrinks across the grain,
and joints that were tight in month one are loose in month eighteen. That is
not a failure; it is what wood does, and it means every joint gets tightened
at least once.

Things get damaged. A member splits, a panel gets hit, water finds a way in.
Replacing one member should not require dismantling a quarter of the building.

Buildings change. A door moves, a window is added, a partition goes in.

WHAT MAKES A CONNECTION REPLACEABLE

Three things, and they are all decisions you make before assembly.

Access. The fastener can be reached with a driver, with the building standing
and the skin on. If it cannot, it is not replaceable no matter what it is made
of.

A thread that does not live in the wood. A screw straight into timber can be
removed and refitted a few times before the hole is chewed. A threaded insert
can be done indefinitely, because the thread is in metal. That is the whole
argument for inserts and it is worth the extra cost per joint.

Standard parts. If the fastener is something you can buy in ten years, the
joint is replaceable. If it is a custom bracket from a supplier who may not
exist, it is not.

THE ORDER OF DISASSEMBLY

A dome comes apart in the reverse of the order it went together, and it is
worth knowing that before you need it.

Top ring first, then down. If you take out a middle ring first, the rings
above it have nothing to stand on.

That is also why the fasteners go on the inside face: at every stage of taking
the dome apart, the joints you need to reach are reachable from inside the
shrinking building.

THE ONE-LINE TEST

Ask of every joint: if this member split tomorrow, what would it take to
replace it?

If the answer is more than an hour and a driver, change the joint now while it
is still a drawing.

chapters.title: 8. Laying Out the Base
chapters.body:
A dome is laid out from one point and one distance. Get those two right and the rest of the site work is bookkeeping.

The rule that runs through this chapter: measure everything from a datum, never from the last thing you measured. Chained measurements accumulate error. A datum does not.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Finding center
sections.body:
Everything on the site is measured from one stake.

Put it in properly, because you cannot move it later without moving the
building.

WHAT THE CENTRE IS

It is the point directly below the apex, and it is the point every base vertex
is the same distance from.

On the reference build every base vertex is 116.4984 inches from it -- the
sphere radius -- measured horizontally along the ground.

HOW TO SET IT

Drive a stake. Put a nail in the top of it, dead centre, and use the nail as
the point rather than the stake. A stake is an inch across; a nail is a point.

Then leave it alone. Everything references it and anything that knocks it
moves the whole building.

WHAT TO CHECK FIRST

Before you commit: stand at the centre and turn round.

Is there room? The dome is 19.416 feet across, which means 9.708 feet in every
direction from where you are standing, plus room to work outside that, plus
room for the eaves of whatever you skin it with.

Check the low side. Ground that looks flat is rarely flat, and a dome needs
its base ring level all the way round.

Check what is above. A dome is 9.708 feet tall at the apex and branches do not
move.

THE THING PEOPLE SKIP

Check the centre against the services.

The reference build brings power, water and drain up through a single port in
the middle of the floor. That port is at the centre stake. If there is a rock,
a root or an existing pipe there, you want to know before the frame is up and
not after.

sections.title: Radius layout
sections.body:
A string and a stake will lay out a dome more accurately than most survey
equipment, provided the string does not stretch.

THE METHOD

Tie a non-stretch line to the centre nail. Mark it at the radius -- 116.4984
inches on the reference build, which is 9 feet 8.5 inches.

Swing it round and scribe a circle.

Every base vertex lands on that circle.

WHY THE LINE MATTERS

Ordinary string stretches. Over nine and a half feet, under the tension you
pull it at, mason's line can add most of an inch -- and it will add a
different amount each time depending on how hard you pull.

Use a steel tape, a fibreglass tape, or a wire. Something that returns the
same number twice.

Better still: use a rigid stick. Cut a piece of timber to exactly the radius,
pivot it on the centre nail, and mark from the end of it. A stick does not
stretch at all, and for a dome this size a stick is entirely practical.

CHECK IT BY CLOSING

Scribe the whole circle and come back to where you started. The line should
meet itself.

If it does not, your pivot has moved, and you should find out why before you
put ten vertices on it.

THE SECOND CHECK

Measure across the circle through the centre. It should be twice the radius:
19.416 feet.

Do that in four directions. All four should agree. If one is different, the
centre is not where you think it is.

Two minutes of checking here prevents a base ring that will not close, which
is a problem you otherwise discover with ten panels built.

sections.title: Polygon/base geometry
sections.body:
The base of a 2V hemisphere is a ten-sided polygon, not a circle.

Ten vertices on the circle, and straight members between them.

THE NUMBERS

Ten base vertices, evenly spaced -- 36 degrees apart around the circle.

Ten base members between them, and on the reference build the base perimeter
is 60.0 feet, which makes each base member 6.0 feet. That is the same as the A
chord, and it is not a coincidence: the base edges of a 2V hemisphere are A
edges.

The polygon encloses 277.0 square feet. The circle through the same ten points
encloses 296.1.

Use the decagon figure for flooring. Use the circle only if you are working
out how much space the dome needs on site.

MARKING THE TEN POINTS

Do not step a chord round the circle with dividers. Error accumulates and the
tenth point will not land on the first.

Two better ways.

Measure the chord: mark one point, measure 6.0 feet along the circle's
circumference to the next, and so on -- but check at the halfway point that
you are diametrically opposite where you started.

Or divide by halving: mark two points at opposite ends of a diameter. Bisect
each half to get four. You cannot get to ten by halving, so this only takes
you so far -- but establishing an accurate diameter first and working from
both ends toward the middle beats stepping round in one direction.

THE CLOSING CHECK

The tenth base member should fit between the tenth vertex and the first
without being cut, forced, or persuaded.

If it does not fit, the error is spread through all ten and you should re-lay
the base rather than absorb it in one joint. A forced base ring pushes its
error up into every ring above it.

sections.title: Foundation interfaces
sections.body:
The frame has to sit on something, and what it sits on has to do three things:
hold it level, keep it off the ground, and hold it down.

LEVEL

Every base vertex at the same height. Not approximately -- a dome is a closed
shape and a base that is out of level puts a twist into the whole frame.

If the ground is not level, the foundation makes up the difference, not the
frame. Do not shim individual members to fix a sloping site.

OFF THE GROUND

Timber in contact with soil rots. Split timber with exposed grain rots faster.

The base members should be clear of the ground with air under them, sitting on
piers, blocks or a deck rather than bearing on soil.

The reference build stands the frame on a framed platform, which puts the base
ring six hundred-odd millimetres clear of the ground with ventilated space
underneath.

HELD DOWN

This is the one people forget.

A dome is light and it is a very good aerofoil. The load case that matters on
a dome is not weight pushing down; it is wind lifting up.

Every base vertex needs a hold-down to the foundation -- a strap, an anchor, a
bolt into the deck. Ten of them.

The reference build uses a strap, ratchet and ground anchor at each of the ten
base vertices, because the soft shell it uses has no stiffness of its own and
the frame carries the whole uplift.

THE INTERFACE ITSELF

Keep it simple and keep it reachable.

A bracket that bolts to the deck and takes the base member with two fasteners
is enough, and it can be inspected and tightened with the building standing.

Anything cast in, buried, or inaccessible is a joint you will never check
again, and this is the joint that stops the building leaving.

sections.title: Leveling
sections.body:
Level the foundation, not the frame.

The frame is a rigid closed shape. If you try to level it by adjusting members
you are distorting the geometry, and the distortion goes somewhere -- usually
into the apex, which will not close.

HOW LEVEL IS LEVEL ENOUGH

Every base vertex within an eighth of an inch of the others.

That is tighter than it sounds and looser than perfectionism. An eighth over
nineteen feet is a very flat platform, and it is achievable with ordinary
tools.

TOOLS THAT WORK

A water level -- two clear tubes and a length of hose -- is accurate over this
span, costs almost nothing, and does not care about line of sight.

A rotary laser is faster if you have one.

A spirit level on a straight edge works for short spans and accumulates error
over long ones. For a nineteen-foot circle, do not chain spirit-level readings
round the perimeter.

THE METHOD

Establish one datum point. Every other point is measured to that datum, not to
its neighbour.

That is the same rule as the members: measure from the master, not from the
last one. Chaining measurements accumulates error; referencing a datum does
not.

Go round twice. The second pass catches the points that moved while you were
working on the others, and there will be some.

CHECK AFTER LOADING

A platform that is level empty may not be level with a dome on it, especially
on soft ground or new fill.

Check again once the base ring is down and before you go up. Settlement that
happens at that stage is easy to shim out. Settlement discovered at the apex
is not.

sections.title: Establishing reference points
sections.body:
A reference point is something you can measure from that will still be there
tomorrow.

You need several, because the centre stake disappears under the building.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH

The centre, marked on the foundation itself rather than only on a stake.

A north line, or any fixed bearing, scribed on the foundation. Every base
vertex is at a known angle from it -- 36 degrees apart -- and it is how you
re-establish the ten points if a mark gets scuffed off.

Two offset points, well outside the building, on that bearing. If the centre
gets covered, two offsets let you find it again by measurement.

The datum height, marked somewhere that will not move. A screw in a nearby
post, a mark on a wall.

WHY THIS IS WORTH TWENTY MINUTES

Halfway through the build you will need to answer a question like "is this
vertex in the right place" and the answer requires measuring from the centre.

The centre, by then, has a floor over it.

If you have offsets you measure from those and get an answer in a minute. If
you do not, you either guess or you take something apart.

WRITE THEM DOWN

On paper, in the shop, not only on the ground.

Radius, datum height, bearing, offset distances. Four numbers. They are the
only things that connect the building to the site, and remembering them is not
a plan.

THE ONE THAT SAVES THE MOST TIME

Mark the ten base vertex positions permanently on the foundation before the
frame goes on -- a screw, a scribe, a paint mark.

Then when a panel does not sit where you expect, you can see immediately
whether the panel is wrong or the layout was.

chapters.title: 9. Assembly
chapters.body:
Assembly is the short part. If the panels are made and checked, raising a nineteen-foot dome is a day or two with two people.

Everything here assumes you built all forty panels first. The method is arranged so that nearly all the work happens flat, at waist height, where it can be checked -- and then the building goes up quickly because there is nothing left to figure out.
chapters.notes:

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: First course
sections.body:
The first course is the ring of triangles sitting on the foundation, and it is
the one that decides whether the rest goes together.

WHAT IT IS

On a 2V hemisphere the bottom course is ten BAB triangles, alternating point
up and point down around the base ring.

Ten panels, and when the tenth one goes in the ring closes on itself.

WHY IT IS THE HARD ONE

Because until it closes, nothing is stable.

Each panel wants to fall inward. There is no completed structure to lean on,
and every joint you make is holding two panels that are themselves being held
by props.

It is also the course where a layout error announces itself. If the base
polygon is out, the tenth panel will not fit, and you will have made nine
joints before finding out.

THE ORDER

Set all ten panels in place, loosely propped, before fastening any of them
permanently.

Do not build round the ring fastening as you go. That is how the accumulated
error ends up entirely in the last joint.

Set them all, check that the ring closes, adjust, and then fasten.

CHECK BEFORE COMMITTING

With all ten standing and loosely held:

* every base vertex on its mark
* the ring closes without forcing
* the top edge of the course is level all the way round
* opposite vertices measure the full diameter, 19.416 feet, in several
  directions

If all four are true, fasten. If any is not, find out why now.

THE HONEST PART

This course takes longer than the four above it put together.

That is normal and it is not a sign you are doing it wrong. The first course
is the one with no structure to help you and the most consequences if it is
out.

sections.title: Triangle assembly
sections.body:
A panel is three members and three pinwheel joints, built flat on a bench.

Build them all before you raise anything.

WHY FLAT AND WHY FIRST

A joint made on a bench, at waist height, with the workpiece held in a jig, is
a better joint than the same joint made overhead on a ladder.

Every joint in this building can be made on a bench. That is not true of most
construction methods and it is one of the genuine advantages here.

So: forty panels, all made flat, all checked, and then an assembly job that is
purely about putting finished things in the right places.

THE SEQUENCE FOR ONE PANEL

Lay the three members in the jig in the pinwheel arrangement. Each one butts
into the side of the next, all going the same way round.

Check the handedness. All forty panels must pinwheel the same direction --
clockwise seen from outside on the reference build. A panel built the other
way is a mirror image and it will not fit anywhere.

Clamp, pilot, fasten. Two or three fasteners per joint.

Take it out of the jig and check it on a flat floor: sits on all three
corners, no rock, sides match the chords.

Label it and stack it.

THE STACK

Stack panels flat, not on edge, and separate the AAAs from the BABs.

Ten of one and thirty of the other. Put them where you can get the one you
want without moving the other twenty-nine, because you will be doing that
forty times.

TIME

About an hour each for the first few. Twenty minutes each once you have the
rhythm.

Forty panels is somewhere between fifteen and twenty-five hours of bench work,
and it is the most pleasant part of the whole build: repetitive, at a
comfortable height, indoors if you want, and entirely checkable.

sections.title: Raising sections
sections.body:
Raising is getting finished panels from the stack into the air and holding
them there until they are fastened.

WHAT IT TAKES

For a nineteen-foot dome: two people and a central prop.

A BAB panel out of six-inch split timber is not light but it is not a
two-person lift either -- one person can carry one. Two people are needed
because one holds while the other fastens.

THE CENTRAL PROP

A post at the centre with an adjustable platform on it.

Each course rests on that platform while it is being fastened. When the course
closes, it is self-supporting and the platform goes up for the next one.

Simple, cheap, and it turns "hold this panel in exactly the right place while
I drive four screws" into "put this panel down on the platform".

ORDER WITHIN A COURSE

Go round the ring in one direction, setting panels loosely.

Do not fasten permanently until the course closes. Same rule as the first
course, for the same reason: an accumulated error should be distributed round
the ring rather than dumped into the last joint.

WHAT NOT TO DO

Do not raise a partly-built course and leave it overnight.

Wind gets into an open dome and an unclosed course is the least stable thing
on the site. Either close the course or brace it properly before you stop.

THE DAY IT TAKES

The raising, for a dome this size, is a day or two with two people -- provided
every panel is already made.

That ratio is the point of the method. Weeks of comfortable bench work, then a
couple of days of assembly. Most of the building happens at waist height.

sections.title: Temporary bracing
sections.body:
Temporary bracing holds the building in the shape it will hold itself in once
it is finished.

Everything here comes out at the end, and every piece of it should be planned
to come out.

WHAT NEEDS BRACING

Each course until it closes.

The whole frame until the apex goes in. A dome without its top ring is an
incomplete arch and it pushes outward at the base.

Any opening. If you are leaving a door or window out of the frame, the panels
either side of the gap have lost a neighbour and need holding.

THE CENTRAL POST

Does most of the work. It carries the courses while they are open and it gives
you something to measure from.

Keep it plumb and keep it in the centre. It is also your reference for whether
the dome is going up straight.

RADIAL BRACES

Timber from the central post out to individual vertices, where a vertex needs
holding at a specific radius.

Use these sparingly. A brace that forces a vertex into position is hiding an
error rather than fixing it -- if a vertex does not want to be where the
geometry says, find out why.

MARK THEM

Use a different colour screw for every temporary fastener.

At the end of the build you have to remove every temporary and leave every
permanent one, and there will be several hundred fasteners in the frame. If
they all look the same you will either leave temporaries in or take permanents
out.

A box of bright screws costs a few pounds and removes an entire category of
end-of-build confusion.

WHEN IT COMES OUT

Top down, after the apex closes and not before.

The dome becomes self-supporting when the last panel goes in. Taking bracing
out from the bottom while the top is open removes the props from under the
part that is still pushing.

sections.title: Course-by-course construction
sections.body:
A 2V hemisphere goes up in three courses and a cap.

THE COURSES

Bottom: ten BAB triangles on the base ring, alternating up and down.

Middle: more BABs, closing the band between the base and the top ring.

Top: the ten AAA triangles, five of which form the ring immediately around the
apex.

Thirty BABs and ten AAAs, in that order, bottom to top.

WHY THIS ORDER

Each course rests on the one below, and each closed course is a rigid ring
that supports the next.

An open course is unstable. A closed one is a compression ring and it will
hold a lot.

So the rhythm is: set a whole course loosely, check it closes, fasten it,
raise the platform, next course.

CHECKING BETWEEN COURSES

Every time a course closes, check three things.

Is it level? The top edge of the completed course should be level all the way
round.

Is it round? Measure across, through the centre, in four directions. All four
should be the same.

Is it the right height? Compare against the geometry. Each course has a known
height and a known radius at its top edge, and the tool will print them.

Those three checks take ten minutes and they stop an error propagating
upward.

WHAT TO DO IF A COURSE WILL NOT CLOSE

Stop. Do not force it.

Measure the panels in that course against each other. If one is different, you
have found it.

If they all match, the error is below -- in the course underneath or in the
base layout -- and forcing this course will push it higher.

A dome that is forced closed at course two has a fight waiting at the apex,
and the apex is the worst place in the building to be arguing with geometry.

sections.title: Apex closure
sections.body:
The last panel is the test of everything.

WHAT HAPPENS AT THE TOP

Five AAA triangles meet at the apex vertex. When the fifth one goes in, the
dome is closed and self-supporting.

Until then it is an arch. After it, it is a dome.

WHY THE LAST PANEL IS DIFFICULT

Because it has no slack.

Every other panel went into a space with one open side. The last one has to go
into a hole that is already bounded on all three sides, and it only fits if
everything below it is right.

That is what makes it such a good test and such a bad surprise.

IF IT DOES NOT FIT

Do not modify the panel.

A panel trimmed to fit the hole is a panel that is now the wrong size, and the
error is still in the building -- it has just moved into the shape of the
frame rather than the gap.

Measure the hole. Compare it to what the geometry says it should be. The
difference tells you how much error has accumulated and, usually, which
direction it came from.

Then loosen the top course, redistribute, and try again. An accumulated error
spread over five joints is invisible. Concentrated in one, it is a gap you can
put your hand through.

WHEN IT DOES FIT

Fasten it, then take the central post out, and stand underneath.

The dome is now holding itself up with nothing in the middle. That is the
moment the method either convinces you or does not, and on a frame that has
gone together properly it is genuinely surprising how solid it feels.

THE PENETRATION

On the reference build the apex is not solid. It carries a sleeve -- the one
hole in the weather surface, with a gasketed cap over it, through which
services leave the building.

If you are building that version, the sleeve goes in with the last panel and
not after. Fitting it later means working at the top of a finished dome, which
is the thing the whole design is arranged to avoid.

sections.title: Alignment correction
sections.body:
Something will be out. This is what to do about it.

FIND OUT WHETHER IT IS ONE THING OR EVERYTHING

Measure three panels from different parts of the dome.

If one is different and two agree, you have a bad panel. Replace it.

If all three differ from the geometry by the same amount in the same
direction, you have a systematic error -- a jig setting, a stop block, a
fence -- and replacing panels will not help because the next one will be wrong
too.

That distinction is the whole of diagnosis and it takes five minutes.

CORRECTING A SINGLE PANEL

Take it out and rebuild it. Do not shim it, pack it, or trim it in place.

A dome is a closed geometry and a panel that is the wrong size is the wrong
size in three directions at once. You cannot fix it with a shim; you can only
move where it is wrong to.

CORRECTING ACCUMULATED ERROR

Spread it.

If a course is half an inch out over ten joints, loosen all ten and let each
one take a twentieth of an inch. Nobody will ever find it.

If you concentrate it in one joint, everybody will find it, starting with you
every time you walk past.

WHEN TO ACCEPT IT

A dome built to a sixteenth is built better than most houses.

If a vertex is a sixteenth off its mark and everything closes, leave it. Wood
moves more than that with the seasons.

If the apex closed, the base ring is level and round, and no joint is held
open, the frame is good. Stop measuring and put the skin on.

THE THING WORTH REMEMBERING

Every error you find in the frame is an error you found before it was covered
up.

That is worth something. The dome is never going to be easier to correct than
it is right now, with nothing on it and every joint reachable from both sides.

chapters.title: 10. Doors, Windows, and Openings
chapters.body:
Every triangle in a dome is carrying something, so every opening is a decision about where its load goes instead.

The structure is usually the easiest part. An opening is also a hole in the envelope, a hole in the insulation, a path for water and an edge that has to be finished, and those four take longer to solve than the framing does.
chapters.notes:

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Removing structural triangles
sections.body:
Every triangle in a dome is carrying something. Take one out and its load goes
to the ones around it.

That is the whole problem with openings, and it is worth stating before any of
the solutions.

WHAT A TRIANGLE ACTUALLY DOES

A geodesic shell works because it is triangulated. A triangle cannot change
shape without changing the length of a side, and the sides are timber, so it
does not change shape.

Remove one and you have left a quadrilateral or worse in the shell -- a shape
that *can* change without stretching anything. It can rack.

The dome does not fall down. The rest of the triangulation is still there and
it is redundant. But the shell around the hole is now doing a different job
than it was designed for, and the members immediately either side of the
opening are the ones doing it.

HOW MANY YOU CAN TAKE

On a 2V hemisphere with forty triangles, taking one is unremarkable. Taking
two adjacent ones is fine with a frame round the hole. Taking three in a row
at the base ring -- which is what turns a dome into a garage -- wants
deliberate reinforcement and is the largest opening this book will describe
without sending you to an engineer.

WHERE TO TAKE THEM

Low, and at the base ring, in preference to anywhere else.

A base triangle has one edge on the ground, which is already an edge with
nothing on the far side of it. Removing one interrupts less than removing a
triangle from the middle of the shell, where five other panels are relying on
it in five directions.

The apex is the worst place. Five triangles meet there and they are all
holding each other.

THE PART THAT IS EASY TO FORGET

An opening is not only a structural hole. It is a hole in the envelope, a hole
in the insulation, a place water can get in, and an edge that has to be
finished.

The structure is usually the easiest of those four to solve.

sections.title: Reinforcing openings
sections.body:
The job of reinforcement is to give the load a path around the hole.

WHAT THAT MEANS PHYSICALLY

The members that used to run through the space now stop at its edge. Whatever
they were carrying has to get to the members that are still continuous, and it
gets there through whatever you put around the opening.

So the reinforcement is a ring. Not a lintel over the top -- a ring all the
way round.

THE SIMPLE VERSION

Double the members that border the opening.

A second stick beside each bordering member, fastened to it along its length,
roughly doubles the section and is the cheapest reinforcement there is. It
costs three or six extra members and an afternoon.

For a single-triangle opening in a 2V hemisphere, that is usually enough.

THE HEADER

For a multi-triangle opening, add a member straight across the top of the
hole, from one continuous vertex to another.

That is a header, it is doing what a header does in a stud wall, and it is the
piece that stops the shell above the opening from settling into it.

Size it generously. A header is one stick and it is carrying what several used
to.

WHAT NOT TO DO

Do not cut a member and leave the cut ends unsupported. A member that stops in
mid-air is not carrying anything and its neighbours are carrying it.

Do not rely on the door or window frame as structure unless you designed it as
structure. A window frame is a weather part.

Do not open the shell in more than one place on the same ring without thinking
about it. Two openings opposite each other on the base ring halve that ring's
ability to act as a compression ring, and the compression ring is what stops
the dome spreading.

THE HONEST LIMIT

Everything above is reasoning, not engineering.

A single triangle out of a forty-triangle shell, with its border doubled, is
within what a careful builder can decide. Three in a row with a header over
them is at the edge of it. More than that, or anything in a place where people
sleep, wants somebody who can put a stamp on it.

sections.title: Door frames
sections.body:
A door is the opening you will use ten times a day for twenty years, and it is
worth more care than any other hole in the building.

WHERE IT GOES

At the base ring, taking one or two triangles.

The base triangles are the only ones where the wall is close to upright, and a
door in a leaning wall is a door you duck through. The dome is 9.708 feet at
the apex and the wall is already tilting in noticeably by the time you are
head height at the perimeter.

That is a real constraint and it is the first thing people are disappointed by.
A nineteen-foot 2V hemisphere does not have a full-height vertical wall
anywhere.

THE EXTENSION ANSWER

The usual solution is not to fight it. Build the door in a small extension --
a porch, a vestibule, a box on the side -- with vertical walls of its own,
joined to the dome at the opening.

That gives you a proper door in a proper frame, a place to take boots off, and
an airlock, which matters more than it sounds in a building with this little
thermal mass.

It also moves the weather detail away from the curved surface, which is the
hardest place to make a door seal.

THE FRAME ITSELF

Build it as a box, independent of the shell, and fix the box to the reinforced
opening.

That way the frame is square even though the hole is triangular, the door is a
normal door, and the joint between the two is a piece of flashing and a gasket
rather than a piece of carpentry nobody has done before.

Do not try to hang a door directly off the dome members. They are at odd
angles, they are split timber with irregular faces, and the door will not stay
square.

THE THRESHOLD

The floor is a platform above ground and the door sill is at platform level.

There will be a step. Plan where it goes and make it a proper step rather than
discovering it at the end, and if the building needs to be accessible, this is
the detail that decides whether it is.

sections.title: Window frames
sections.body:
Windows are easier than doors, because nothing walks through them and they can
follow the shell's geometry instead of fighting it.

THE TRIANGLE WINDOW

The simplest window in a wedge dome is a glazed panel in a bay.

The bay is already a frame -- three members with a lip cut into them by the
shape of the wedge. Put a triangular pane in instead of a solid panel and you
have a window with no new framing at all.

That is the option the reference build uses, and it is why the fit-out
catalogue can turn a dome into a studio by changing which bays are glazed.

WHAT IT COSTS YOU

Triangular glass is a special order and it is more expensive per square foot
than rectangular.

It does not open. A triangular opening light is possible and it is not a
standard product.

And a triangle high in the shell is a skylight whether you meant it or not --
it faces upward, it gets sun all day, and it leaks heat all night.

THE OPENING WINDOW

If you want a window that opens, put a square one in a square sub-frame inside
a triangular opening, the same way the door goes in a box.

You lose some glass area to the frame. You gain a normal window with normal
hardware that a normal person can replace in fifteen years.

WHERE TO PUT THEM

Low for view, high for light.

A dome's upper panels face the sky and will light the room brilliantly and
overheat it in summer. The lower panels face out and give you something to
look at.

Most people want more of the second than they expect and fewer of the first.

THE SEAL

Every window is a hole in the envelope with a perimeter, and on a curved shell
that perimeter is not in one plane.

That is the detail to get right, and the way to make it easy is the same as
everywhere else in this book: make the opening flat and local -- a sub-frame
-- and seal to the sub-frame rather than to the curve.

sections.title: Entry extensions
sections.body:
An entry extension is a small structure joined to the dome at an opening, and
it solves several problems at once.

WHAT IT SOLVES

A vertical door, in a building with no vertical walls.

An airlock, in a building with very little thermal mass, where opening the
door in January dumps the room's heat in ten seconds.

Somewhere to leave boots, coats and firewood, in a round room with no corners
and no hallway.

And a place to put the weather detail, off the curved surface.

WHAT IT IS

A box. Stud-framed, or built from the same wedge members if you want the
consistency, with a flat roof or a small pitch, joined to the dome around a
reinforced opening.

It does not need to be big. Four feet deep is enough for a door, a step and a
pair of boots.

THE JOINT

This is the only difficult part and it is the same difficulty as any roof
penetration: a flat thing meeting a curved thing.

Two approaches.

Flash it. Treat the joint like a chimney flashing -- an apron under the shell
covering above, sealed at the top, open at the bottom so anything that gets
behind it drains out.

Or gasket it. Build the extension with a collar cut to the dome's curve, and
compress a gasket between the two. This is tidier, more expensive, and depends
on the collar being accurate.

The reference build's shell is removable, which makes the second option
awkward -- anything gasketed to the shell has to come off with it. So: flash
to the frame, not to the shell, and let the shell overlap.

THE THING WORTH SAYING

An extension makes the dome look less like a dome.

Some people mind that a great deal. If you are one of them, the answer is a
door straight into the shell and a life of ducking, and that is a legitimate
choice as long as it is a choice rather than a surprise.

sections.title: Avoiding weak discontinuities
sections.body:
A discontinuity is any place the shell stops being a shell -- an opening, a
join, a change of material, a place where the triangulation is interrupted.

They are not avoidable. They are manageable, and the management is mostly
about not putting them next to each other.

THE RULES THAT MATTER

Do not stack them. Two openings in the same vertical line, one above the
other, leave a strip of shell with nothing bracing it sideways.

Do not mirror them. Two large openings directly opposite each other across the
dome halve the base ring's ability to work as a compression ring -- and it is
the compression ring that stops the dome spreading at the bottom.

Do not cluster them. Three openings within a few panels of each other make one
large weak region rather than three small ones.

Spread them round. If you need four windows, put them at roughly 90 degrees to
each other rather than in a row.

THE APEX

Leave it alone.

Five triangles meet at the top and they are the most interdependent group in
the building. The reference build puts one penetration there -- a gasketed
sleeve for services -- and that is a hole through a panel, not a missing
panel.

THE BASE RING

The base ring is a compression ring and it is the single most important
continuous element in the dome. It is what turns outward thrust into hoop
stress and stops the dome spreading.

Interrupting it is the one thing to avoid if you can. A door that takes a base
triangle interrupts the panels but should not interrupt the ring member itself
-- keep the member at the bottom continuous and take the opening out above it,
with a threshold over the member.

That is a small detail and it is worth more than most of the reinforcement in
this chapter.

THE TEST

Walk round the finished frame and look for any place where you could push the
shell sideways and it would move.

If there is one, that is a discontinuity that needs bracing. If there is not,
the openings you have cut are fine.

parts.title: Part IV - Turning the Frame Into a Building

chapters.title: 11. Panels and Shells
chapters.body:
The frame holds the building up. The skin keeps the weather out. They are separate jobs and this method keeps them separate, which is why the skin can be changed without touching the structure.

One number governs the whole chapter: no panel of this dome fits on a four-foot sheet in any rotation. The narrowest is 52.520 inches and a sheet is 48. Everything about how the skin gets built follows from that.
chapters.notes:
CHAPTER GOAL: Build a practical, illustrated chapter covering 11. Panels and Shells.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Plywood
sections.body:
Plywood is the default and it has one problem on this building, which is worth
getting out of the way first.

NO PANEL FITS A SHEET

The narrowest panel in a 2V hemisphere on a six-foot member is 52.520 inches
across its shortest altitude. The widest AAA panel is 62.354.

A sheet of plywood is 48 inches wide.

There is no rotation, no nesting and no clever layout that gets a panel of
this dome out of a standard sheet. The narrowest one is four and a half inches
too wide.

That is not a small inconvenience. It decides how the entire skin gets built,
and it is the sort of thing that is obvious in a car park and invisible on a
drawing.

WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT

Three options.

Buy oversized sheet. Some suppliers carry 5x10 or 4x10; a 60-inch sheet takes
a BAB panel and a 5-foot sheet takes both. It is a special order and it costs
more per square foot.

Sheet across the frame. Run ordinary sheets over several panels at once,
following the curve in facets, and cut at the frame lines. You get joints in
the middle of panels instead of at their edges, which is structurally
irrelevant and visually obvious.

Build the panel up from boards. Narrower stock, laid edge to edge inside the
bay. More labour, no special order, and it looks like a timber building rather
than a sheet-goods building.

THE REFERENCE BUILD

Sheets across the frame, taped at the joints, because it is the option that
does not require anybody to order anything unusual.

GRADE AND GLUE

If it is inside the envelope and dry, interior-grade is fine.

If it is outside, or if it is part of the removable shell that lives in the
weather, it wants exterior glue at minimum and marine ply if you can afford
it. The failure mode of the wrong glue is delamination, and delamination on a
curved surface is not repairable.

sections.title: Composite panels
sections.body:
A composite panel is two skins with a core between them, and the core is doing
most of the work.

WHY THEY SUIT A DOME

A dome panel is a triangle spanning about five feet, carrying wind and snow
and its own weight, and it is not carrying the building -- the frame does
that.

That is exactly the load case a composite is good at: stiff across a span,
light, and not required to be strong in the way a structural member is.

THE COMMON CORES

Foam. Light, insulating, cheap, and it will not take a fastener. Anything
screwed to it needs a hard insert.

Honeycomb. Stiffer for its weight than foam, more expensive, and it does not
insulate.

Timber. A ply skin either side of a timber frame is the oldest composite there
is and the one you can make in a shed.

THE JOIN PROBLEM

Composites are excellent panels and awkward edges.

A foam-cored panel has an exposed core all the way round, which has to be
capped, sealed or rebated. On a triangle that is three edges per panel and 120
edges for the dome.

That edge detail is where composite panels get expensive, and it is the reason
people who cost a composite skin off the panel price alone are always
surprised.

WHERE THEY EARN IT

Where you want insulation and structure in one operation and you are not
planning to take the panel off again.

The reference build does not use them, because the reference build's whole
argument is a shell that comes off and layers that stack underneath. A
composite panel decides its own insulation value at the factory and cannot
change its mind afterwards.

That is the trade: a composite is better on the day it goes on, and it is the
last decision you get to make about that bay.

sections.title: Fiberglass
sections.body:
Glass fibre in resin is the material the reference build's hard shell is made
of, and it is worth understanding because it sets the cost ceiling for the
whole building.

WHAT IT IS

Cloth -- woven or stitched glass -- wetted out with a resin that cures hard.
Layers build thickness. A core between layers makes it stiff without making it
heavy.

HOW IT IS PRICED

By weight, not by area. Ounces of glass per square foot, times a
resin-to-glass ratio.

That is the industry's own method and it is the thing most amateur costings
get wrong. A rule of thumb in resin-per-square-foot will be right for one
schedule and wrong for every other.

WATCH THE UNITS. Woven and stitched fabrics are sold by ounces per square
*yard*. Chopped strand mat is sold by ounces per square *foot*. Getting that
backwards understates a laminate by a third.

WHAT IT COSTS ON THIS DOME

Over 1,325 square feet of laminate, four named systems:

* sheathed ply in epoxy: $5,395
* boatyard polyester: $6,045
* premium marine polyester: $6,668
* vinyl ester: $9,144

That is the most expensive line in the building by a wide margin -- more than
the frame, the core, the services and the fit-out together.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH DESCRIBING

Because it is a sixty-year object.

A gelcoated hull outlives every other option in this chapter several times
over, it is genuinely waterproof rather than nearly waterproof, and it is a
trade with real suppliers, real published prices and sixty years of people
knowing how to do it.

THE ARGUMENT AGAINST, WHICH THE NEXT CHAPTER MAKES PROPERLY

It is made once, at one size, and it cannot grow.

The cavity behind it holds four quilted layers and then it is full. After that,
insulating further means losing floor area or building a second shell outside
the first, and neither happens.

So the hull quietly caps how good the building is ever allowed to get. That is
the problem the shower cap exists to solve.

sections.title: Metal
sections.body:
Sheet metal over a dome is common, cheap and worth knowing the failure modes
of.

WHAT IT IS GOOD AT

Water. A metal roof sheds it and keeps shedding it for decades.

Fire. In a place where that matters, nothing else in this chapter compares.

Cost per square foot, if you buy it flat and cut it yourself.

WHAT IT IS BAD AT

Compound curves. A dome is not a cone and it is not a cylinder: you cannot
wrap flat sheet round it without either cutting it into small facets or
stretching it.

Small facets means a great many pieces and a great many laps.

Noise. Rain on metal over an uninsulated shell is memorable, and a dome is a
very good acoustic reflector -- it focuses sound at the centre of the room.

Heat. Uninsulated metal in sun radiates into the space below it.

Condensation. Metal is cold, inside air is damp, and the underside of a metal
sheet is where that meets. Without a vented cavity or a vapour control layer
you get water dripping off the inside of the roof and everybody blames the
roof for leaking.

THE PANEL-BY-PANEL APPROACH

The one that suits this dome: a flat triangle of sheet per bay, fixed to the
frame with the edges lapped or capped at the seams.

Forty pieces, all one of two shapes, all flat. That is a manageable job and it
fits the method's logic of doing everything forty times.

THE DETAIL THAT DECIDES IT

The seams. Forty triangles is 120 edges, of which 55 are interior seams where
two panels meet at a dihedral angle.

Every one of those is a lap that has to shed water downhill and accommodate a
fold of 18 or 22 degrees. Get the seam detail right and metal is excellent.
Get it wrong and you have 55 places for water to get in.

sections.title: Transparent panels
sections.body:
Glazing a dome is easy to overdo and easy to get wrong in one specific way.

THE OPTIONS

Glass. Best optically, heaviest, most expensive, and a special order in
triangles.

Polycarbonate, twin-wall or solid. Light, tough, insulating in the twin-wall
form, and it yellows and goes brittle under UV unless it has a coated face --
and the coated face has to go outward, which people get wrong.

Acrylic. Clearer than polycarbonate, more brittle, scratches easily.

Polyester or PVC corrugated sheet. Cheap, agricultural, and short-lived.

WHERE TO PUT THEM

Low, mostly.

A dome's upper panels face the sky. A glazed panel up there is a skylight: it
will light the room beautifully, cook it in summer and lose heat all night.
The reference build's own performance model finds the shape is already worth
41 percent less envelope than a box, and putting glass in the top gives a
chunk of that back.

Lower panels face outward and give you a view, which is usually what people
actually wanted.

THE THERMAL PROBLEM

Any glazing is a hole in the insulation.

A single-glazed panel is roughly R-1. A quilted layer is R-1.6, and the
reference build's seven-layer stack is R-12.7. So one glazed bay undoes rather
a lot of stacked quilt.

That is not a reason to avoid glass. It is a reason to count the bays.

THE ONE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE

A dome is a reflector. A curved glazed surface facing a room concentrates
light and heat toward the centre, and in a small dome the centre is where you
are standing.

Two or three glazed bays are pleasant. Eight is a greenhouse, and it will
behave like one.

sections.title: Insulated panels
sections.body:
An insulated panel puts the insulation in the bay rather than on top of the
shell, and that is a real architectural choice rather than a detail.

THE BAY AS A CAVITY

The wedge gives you the cavity for free.

Because the member's inward face stands proud of where the panel sits, every
bay has a lip already cut into it by the shape of a split log -- three-quarters
of an inch on the reference build. An inner panel drops onto that lip, and
behind it is a cavity as deep as the member: six inches.

Forty bays of six-inch cavity is a substantial volume of insulation if you
want it there.

WHY THE REFERENCE BUILD SHIPS IT EMPTY

Two reasons, and the first is the honest one: money. A dome that ships
insulated is a dome that costs more on day one, and the campaign's entire
argument is a low entry price.

The second is better. An empty cavity is a duct, and the seam channels connect
all forty of them. Fill the bays and you lose the airflow experiment
completely.

WHAT GOES IN, IF ANYTHING DOES

Quilted recycled fabric, a layer at a time. Roughly R-1.6 a layer.

Blown cellulose, if you accept that it settles and that you will never get it
out again.

Rigid foam, cut to triangles. Best performance per inch, most waste, and
forty triangles of offcut.

Nothing. Which is a legitimate answer for a workshop, a store or a summer
building.

THE DECISION UNDERNEATH

An insulated panel decides its R-value at the factory. A cavity you can open
does not.

This book's bias is toward the second, and it is the same bias that runs
through the whole method: prefer the thing you can change your mind about.

sections.title: Removable panels
sections.body:
A panel you can take off is a different object from a panel you screwed on,
and the difference shows up in year three rather than on the day.

WHY REMOVABLE

Because the cavity behind it is where the insulation goes, and the insulation
is bought a layer at a time over years.

Because a panel gets damaged and replacing one should not mean dismantling
six.

Because a bay's *function* changes -- a blank becomes a window, a window
becomes an exhaust, a solid panel becomes a solar bay -- and the whole
fit-out argument depends on that being an afternoon's work.

HOW THE REFERENCE BUILD DOES IT

The panel sits on the *outside* face of the frame and is pulled into it by
screws landing in threaded inserts set in the wedges.

Four inserts per bay, 160 for the dome.

That arrangement matters more than it sounds. The older version had the panel
compression-fitted into the bay from outside, held by friction -- and most of
a dome's bays are overhead, so a friction fit overhead spends the life of the
building arguing with gravity.

Screwed in, gravity works with the fixing. And the panel comes off with a
driver rather than a pry bar.

THE SECOND JOB THE INSERTS DO

They are a grid of structural anchor points on a known pitch.

Three inserts together hold about 540 pounds, which means a shelf, a bunk, a
hanging rail or a kitchen run can span two or three triangles and bolt to
them.

So a bay does not have to be *used* to be useful. It is a barrier with fixings
in it, and that is worth more than the panel.

THE COST

Inserts and flange screws come to a couple of hundred dollars across the dome,
and about four hours of build time to set them.

That is the price of every future change to the building being a driver job.

sections.title: Snap-in concepts
sections.body:
A snap-in panel goes in without tools. It is the direction this method is
heading and it is not where the reference build is yet, so this section is
honest about which is which.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT WORK

A gasket that compresses when the panel is pushed home, and a catch that holds
it against the gasket's spring.

That is a door seal, and door seals are a solved problem -- but they are solved
on rectangular doors in rigid frames, and this is a triangle in a frame made
of split logs.

THE PROBLEM THAT HAS TO BE SOLVED FIRST

Split timber is not dimensionally identical bay to bay.

A snap fitting needs the opening to be the same size every time, to within a
millimetre or two, or the catch either does not reach or does not release.

Forty bays made from real trees are not that consistent, and making them that
consistent means machining the inside faces of every member -- which is
exactly the work the wedge method exists to avoid.

THE HONEST POSITION

Snap-in is the right answer for a manufactured panel in a manufactured frame.

For a frame split out of a buyer's own trees, screws into inserts are the
right answer, and the four screws per bay are not the thing slowing anybody
down.

WHAT IS WORTH BORROWING FROM THE IDEA ANYWAY

Captive fasteners. A screw that stays in the panel when it is undone means no
bag of screws to lose and no dropped fastener at the top of a dome.

A single-handed catch at one corner, with screws at the others, so a panel can
be held with one hand while the first fixing goes in.

Both of those give you most of the convenience without needing the frame to be
machine-consistent.

The reference build should probably do the first. It does not yet.
