sections.title: Weather seals
sections.body:
The dome has 55 interior seams, 10 base edges, one apex penetration and
however many openings you cut. Every one of them is a place water can get in.

THE GENERAL RULE

Shed, do not seal.

A detail that relies on a bead of sealant is a detail with a maintenance
schedule. A detail where water runs downhill, over a lap, and away needs
nothing from anybody for twenty years.

Use sealant as a backup to a shed detail, never as the detail.

THE SEAM

This is the interesting one, because the reference build does something
unusual with it.

Two sawn faces meeting at a dihedral angle do not close flush. There is a
wedge-shaped gap along every one of the 55 interior seams -- 309 feet of it,
reaching every vertex.

Every other way of building a dome machines that out. The reference build caps
it and uses it: as a conduit for services, and as an air duct, blown to keep
the frame dry or drawn to take what lands on the shell down into a tank.

So the seam detail is not only a weather detail. It is a channel with a cap on
it, and the cap is doing the shedding.

THE SHELL OVERLAP

The removable shell lands on the *frame*, not on the panels, and it overlaps
every seam.

That is what makes the seams a secondary line of defence rather than the
primary one. The shell sheds; the seams catch what gets past.

Two lines is the whole strategy and it is the same one used in the shower: an
inner barrier that takes the spray and an outer one that catches what gets
through.

THE APEX

One penetration in the whole weather surface, closed by a gasketed cap with
over-centre catches.

Meant to stay shut for years and come off in ten minutes. Every service that
gets added later leaves under that cap and runs down the outside, so nothing
ever cuts a new hole in a weathertight surface.

That is the single best weather decision in the building and it is worth
protecting. Do not let anybody drill the shell.

chapters.title: 12. Floor and Foundation Systems
chapters.body:
A dome puts its whole weight on ten points of a circle and nothing in between, which makes most of what is known about foundations slightly wrong for it.

Every figure in this chapter is for the same 22.4-foot pad, priced off the same takeoff the campaign film reads from, so the five options can be compared against each other rather than against somebody's memory of a quote.
chapters.notes:

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Slab
sections.body:
A concrete slab is the most expensive foundation in this chapter and the only
one that is also the finished floor.

WHAT IT COSTS

$2,468 under a 22.4-foot dome.

That is the whole platform: excavation, gravel, forms, reinforcement,
concrete and finishing. It is not the cheapest and it is not far off the
framed alternatives, because a slab has no timber in it and timber is what
the others spend their money on.

WHAT YOU GET FOR IT

A floor. Nothing else on this list is a floor -- the others are platforms
that a floor goes on top of, and that second floor is a cost the comparison
tends to forget.

Thermal mass. A slab holds heat and gives it back, which in a building with
as little mass as a timber dome is worth having in some climates and a
liability in others.

Permanence. It does not rot, it does not move, and it does not need looking
at again.

WHAT IT COSTS YOU

The dome can never move. That is the whole trade, and in a method built
around a building you can take apart, it is a large thing to give up.

Services are cast in. What you did not put in the pour, you cut for later.

It is a contractor job, or a very organised weekend with help. Concrete does
not wait for you to think.

Damp, if there is no membrane. Put one in.

WHEN TO CHOOSE IT

When the building is never moving, when the climate rewards mass, and when
you want the floor and the foundation to be one purchase rather than two.

Otherwise, read on.

sections.title: Ring foundation
sections.body:
A ring foundation is concrete where the load lands and lumber where it does
not, and on a dome that turns out to be most of the floor.

THE REASON IT SUITS THIS BUILDING

A 2V dome delivers its whole weight to ten points on a circle.

Not to a perimeter wall, not to the middle -- ten points, evenly spaced,
where the base vertices sit. Everything inside that circle is carrying
furniture and people, which is a fraction of the load and a job timber does
perfectly well.

So pouring the middle is pouring concrete that nothing stands on.

WHAT IT COSTS

$3,039 for the ring and the framed middle, on 82 boards
of lumber.

That is more than the slab's $2,468 -- and that is worth saying plainly
rather than hiding, because the intuition is that half a pour must be cheaper
than a whole one. It is not. The saving on concrete is smaller than the cost
of the timber deck that replaces it, and the ring's formwork is fiddlier per
cubic yard than a slab's.

WHAT YOU ACTUALLY BUY

A floor you can get under.

That is the thing. Services run in the void, they stay reachable, and a
mistake is an afternoon rather than a demolition saw. On a slab every pipe
is a decision you made once.

It is also the honest way to build on ground that is not flat, because the
ring can step and the deck inside it stays level.

WHO ELSE BUILDS THIS WAY

Grain bins and yurt platforms, both of which are round buildings that put
their load on a perimeter. It is not an invention; it is the standard answer
to this shape, arrived at by people who were not thinking about domes.

WHEN TO CHOOSE IT

When you want permanence at the load points and access everywhere else, and
when the ground is uneven enough that a slab would need a lot of fill.

Not for the money. It does not save any.

sections.title: Pier foundation
sections.body:
Piers are the cheapest permanent thing you can put a building on, and for a
dome they are close to ideal.

WHY

Ten load points. Ten piers. There is nothing in between for a foundation to
do.

A dome does not need a continuous footing because it does not have a
continuous wall. Every other building on a pier foundation is compromising;
this one is matching.

WHAT IT COSTS

$2,916 for piers, beams, joists and a sealed 2x6 deck --
116 boards.

That is the reference build's staple and the bare minimum that hosts a dome.
Two people and a weekend.

Add $4,263 if you want a floor you can mop: the same platform
with plywood and epoxy over it. The ply is not optional. Epoxy over gapped
deck boards cracks at every joint, every time.

WHAT A PIER IS

A precast block on compacted gravel, a poured footing, a screw pile, or a
treated post in the ground, in rising order of cost and permanence.

Blocks on gravel are what the reference build prices, because they are what
somebody can actually buy on a Saturday.

THE TWO THINGS THAT GO WRONG

Frost. A pier that does not reach below the frost line will lift, and it will
lift unevenly, and a dome on an uneven ring racks. Know your depth.

Settlement. Ten piers on undisturbed, compacted ground settle together. Ten
piers where one sits on backfill settle nine ways. Compact properly or find
different ground.

WHEN TO CHOOSE IT

Almost always, for a first building. It is cheap, it is quick, the dome can
leave, and everything under the floor stays reachable.

sections.title: Raised deck
sections.body:
A raised deck is a pier foundation with the piers made taller, and it changes
what the building is.

WHAT IT BUYS

Level, on ground that is not.

Airflow underneath, which on a timber building in a wet climate is worth more
than most of the things people spend money on instead.

Height, which gets the floor above snow, above runoff, and above the wildlife
that would otherwise investigate the underside.

Storage and services in the void, at a height you can stand in rather than
crawl through.

WHAT IT COSTS

Above the $2,916 for the standard platform, the extra is posts,
bracing and a stair. Height is cheap in material and expensive in the bracing
it demands -- a deck two feet up needs almost none, and one six feet up needs
diagonal bracing in both directions or it will sway.

THE THING THAT CATCHES PEOPLE

A tall deck is a structure in its own right and it wants engineering the dome
above it does not.

The dome is a triangulated shell that resolves its own loads. A post-and-beam
platform under it is a frame that racks, and the taller it gets the more of a
problem that is. The dome will not save it.

Brace it properly, in both directions, and do not let the bracing stop at the
fun part.

THE DETAIL WORTH GETTING RIGHT

A step is not a stair. Anything over about eighteen inches needs real treads,
real risers and a handrail, and putting that in at the start is a fraction of
the cost of retrofitting it after somebody falls.

sections.title: Portable platform
sections.body:
A platform that comes apart is the foundation that matches a building that
comes apart, and it is the least-built option on this list for reasons that
are mostly habit.

WHAT IT IS

A deck built in panels, bolted together, sitting on adjustable feet or blocks
rather than anything poured.

Four to ten panels for a 22.4-foot pad. Two people carry a panel. The
whole thing goes together in a morning and comes apart in an afternoon.

WHAT IT COSTS

Broadly the $2,916 of the framed platform, plus the hardware that
makes the joints demountable and minus the piers you no longer pour.

It is not cheaper. It is *reversible*, which is a different kind of value and
the one this method keeps reaching for.

WHERE IT EARNS ITS KEEP

Rented land. A platform that leaves no trace is a platform a landowner will
say yes to.

Permitting. In many places a structure on a non-permanent foundation is a
different animal from one on a poured footing, and the difference is
sometimes the difference between allowed and not. Ask locally; do not assume.

Trial siting. Put the dome where you think you want it, live with it a
season, and move it fifty feet when you find out you were wrong about the
morning sun.

THE COMPROMISES

It moves. Adjustable feet need adjusting, seasonally, and somebody has to
remember.

It does not like slopes. Every inch of fall is another inch of adjustment
range you need at one edge.

And the services have to be demountable too, which is easy if the design
allowed for it and infuriating if it did not. The reference build's utility
core exists partly for this reason.

sections.title: Prepared building pad
sections.body:
The pad is what goes under every other option here, and it is the one people
skip.

WHAT IT IS

Strip the topsoil. Cut and fill to level. Compact. Lay graded stone.
Compact again. Drain away from the building.

WHAT IT COSTS

$443 for a 22.4-foot pad.

That is the cheapest line in this whole chapter by a factor of five, and it
is the one that decides whether any of the others work.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE THING ON TOP

Every foundation on this list transmits its load into the ground. If the
ground moves, the foundation moves, and it does not matter what the
foundation is made of.

Uncompacted fill settles. It settles for years, it settles unevenly, and a
dome on an uneven base ring racks -- which shows up as doors that stop
closing and panels that will not sit in their bays.

Concrete does not fix bad ground. It spreads the load over more of it, which
helps, and then cracks where the ground moved anyway.

DRAINAGE IS THE OTHER HALF

Water under a building is what turns settled ground into moving ground.

Fall away from the pad in every direction. A swale uphill if the site has
one. Gutters, if there is anything to catch.

None of it is expensive and all of it is boring, which is exactly why it gets
left out.

THE HONEST SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

Cheapest to dearest, on the same 22.4-foot pad:

* gravel base only: $443 -- not a floor, and nobody lives on it
* full concrete slab: $2,468 -- and it *is* the floor
* framed deck on piers, sealed: $2,916 -- the staple
* concrete ring, timber middle: $3,039
* framed deck, ply and epoxy: $4,263 -- a floor you can mop

Two things in that list are worth stopping on. The slab is not the expensive
option people assume, because it is the only one that does not then need a
floor built on it. And the ring, which sounds like it ought to be the clever
economy, costs more than the slab it half-replaces.

Neither of those is the answer the argument wanted. They are what the takeoff
says.

chapters.title: 13. Utilities
chapters.body:
A conventional house runs its services in wall cavities. A dome does not have a wall cavity, and the attempts to pretend it does are where most of the trouble comes from.

This method puts everything in one column standing in the middle of the building -- $1,405 of it, in through one port in the floor and out through one sleeve at the apex. Three designed penetrations in the whole envelope, all of them gasketed, none of them cut later.
chapters.notes:

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Electrical entry
sections.body:
Electricity comes into this building at one point, low, and goes up.

WHERE

The floor port, in the middle of the pad, under the dome.

Not through a wall. A dome does not have a wall in the sense a service entry
wants -- every surface is curved, sloping and part of the weather envelope,
and a penetration through it is a penetration through the roof.

The middle of the floor is flat, sheltered, and already where everything else
arrives.

WHAT IT IS

A sub-panel with breakers and an outlet ring, priced at
$310 in the reference build. That is the
equipment, not the supply.

The supply is somebody else's number: a spur from a meter, a generator, a
battery bank, or the shared hub the campaign film prices at a quarter of a
four-way panel. Which of those you have changes the cost by thousands and
changes nothing about the dome.

THE RULE THAT MATTERS

Everything electrical goes up the column, and the column is metal and
grounded.

That gives you one chase, one route, and one place to look. The alternative
-- cable run round the inside of a curved shell -- is how you end up drilling
into something you should not have.

SEPARATION

Water rises in the same column. They are in the same object and they are not
in the same chase: the electrical side is its own conduit with its own
clearance, and the wet side drains downward past it.

Three feet of clearance between the electrical and anything wet is the
reference build's rule, and it is the one number in this chapter nobody
should shave.

sections.title: Water entry
sections.body:
Water arrives where the electricity does: at the pad port, in the middle of
the floor, and rises from there.

THE MANIFOLD

A water manifold and rise from the pad, $240.

One inlet, one shut-off, and branches off it at working height. That is the
whole thing, and the reason it is one object rather than a run of pipe is so
that disconnecting the dome from the pad is one action.

WHERE IT COMES FROM

Four honest options, in rising order of independence:

A spur from a mains supply. Cheapest to run, most dependent.

A tank, filled by truck or hose. The reference build prices
120 gallons under the floor at
$1.35 a gallon of capacity, which is a few
hundred dollars and buys a week or two depending entirely on how you live.

Rainwater off the shell. A dome is a very good catchment -- it is a smooth
curved surface with a single low edge -- and the seam network can be run as
the collector.

A well. Different chapter, different trade, and the only one on this list
that needs a rig.

FREEZING

A pipe in an unheated void freezes. The under-floor space is an unheated
void.

Either the tank and the rise are inside the insulated envelope, or they are
heat-traced, or the system drains down when the building is empty. Pick one
deliberately. Discovering in February which one you picked by accident is a
bad afternoon.

sections.title: Plumbing
sections.body:
Waste is the part of a small building people plan last and regret first.

THE DRAIN STACK

A drain stack and floor-port tie-in, $165.

Everything wet in the dome drains to the middle of the floor and out through
the pad. That is the opposite of a conventional building, where waste runs to
a wall and out sideways -- and it is the right way round here, because the
middle of the floor is the only place the geometry guarantees is reachable.

FALL

Waste moves because it is running downhill, and in a building on a platform
there is not much downhill available.

A quarter-inch of fall per foot is the number, and the shower tray in the
reference build's wet area is built to exactly that over a three-foot run.
Under a quarter-inch the water moves and the solids do not, which is the
failure people describe as "the drain keeps blocking" and is actually "the
drain was never going to work".

WHERE IT GOES

Off the pad and into whatever the site has: a sewer connection, a septic
field, a holding tank, or a greywater system with a composting toilet
handling the rest.

That last combination is the one that suits this building best, because it
halves the waste problem and removes the one part of it that needs treating.

THE WET AREA

Water and electricity in the same small round room is the thing to design
rather than hope about.

The reference build's answer: a sloped tray that redirects to the drain, two
barriers round the shower rather than one -- a double glass wall or a double
curtain -- and three feet of clearance between anything wet and anything
electrical.

Two barriers is not belt and braces. The inner one takes the spray and the
outer one catches what gets past, which is the same two-line strategy the
shell uses against rain.

sections.title: Central utility column
sections.body:
The utility column is the single best idea in this building and the one
hardest to explain on paper.

WHAT IT IS

A metal column standing in the middle of the dome, floor to apex, carrying
everything: water up, waste down, electrical up, and out through the top.

Priced at $1,405 complete, over 6.5 hours to
assemble on a bench.

WHY THE MIDDLE

Because a dome has no good walls and one excellent middle.

Every service in a conventional house runs in a wall cavity. A dome's
equivalent of a wall cavity is a triangular bay in a curved shell, and
running services there means they follow the curve, cross the seams, and end
up somewhere different from where you left them.

The middle is vertical, straight, and the same at every height.

WHY IT IS ONE OBJECT

Because then it can leave.

The column unbolts from the pad port at the bottom and the apex sleeve at the
top, and goes into the next dome. The campaign film prices that move at
$260 and rates the core for
25 years, which is longer than most of the
buildings it will stand in.

That is the modular argument, and it only works because the services are one
thing rather than forty things buried in a shell.

WHAT IS ON IT

The housing and apex sleeve, $380. The water
manifold. The drain stack. The sub-panel. A service chase running
10.5 feet from floor to apex at
$11 a foot. And the seal cap over the apex
penetration at $195.

Six items. That is the entire service infrastructure of the building, and
you can walk round it.

sections.title: Utility routing through the floor
sections.body:
Everything arrives through one hole in the floor, and that hole is the most
important detail in the building's services.

THE PORT

A service port up through the deck, $340.

One opening, lined, sealed to the deck, with the water, waste and electrical
passing through it and the column landing on top of it.

WHY ONE HOLE

Because a hole in a floor is a place for air, water and animals, and one of
them is manageable.

Also because the dome has to be able to leave. Lift it off and what is left
is one capped port in a platform, not a scattering of stubs.

THE VOID UNDERNEATH

On a framed platform there is a crawl space, and everything upstream of the
port lives in it: the tank, the incoming spur, the shut-off, the drain run
out to wherever it goes.

That space is unheated, so see the freezing note two sections back, and it is
where the reference build puts $420 of storage
because the space exists whether you use it or not.

On a slab, none of this is true. Everything is cast in, it is in its final
position, and the crawl space does not exist. That is the slab's real cost
and it does not appear in its price.

THE ONE THING TO GET RIGHT

Seal the port to the floor, not to the column.

The column comes out. If the seal belongs to the column, taking the column
out opens the floor. If it belongs to the floor, the floor stays closed and
the column lifts through it.

sections.title: Apex routing
sections.body:
The top of the dome is a socket, and everything the building grows later
leaves through it.

WHAT IS UP THERE

A sleeve through the apex panel, the riser passing through it, and a gasketed
seal cap over the lot, $195.

The riser does not stop at the apex. It stands proud of it, and the part
standing proud is the interface: a place a line can be picked up from outside
without opening the building.

WHY THIS IS WORTH THE TROUBLE

Because it means nothing ever cuts a new hole in a weathertight surface.

Solar goes on later, and it comes down from the apex. A satellite dish, an
aerial, a weather station, a vent, a flue for a stove that was not there
originally: all of them leave under the cap and run down the outside.

The alternative -- one penetration per addition -- is how a roof becomes a
leak.

THE CAP

Gasketed, with over-centre catches, meant to stay shut for years and come off
in ten minutes.

It is the single best weather decision in the building, and the one to
protect. Anyone who drills the shell to save walking a cable up has undone
it.

THE PART PEOPLE DOUBT

A hole in the highest point of a roof sounds like the worst possible place
for one.

It is the best, for the same reason a boat's deck fittings are on the high
side: water does not collect there. A penetration halfway down the curve sits
in the path of everything running off the surface above it. The apex has
nothing above it.

sections.title: Exterior routing
sections.body:
Once a line is outside the shell, it runs down the outside, and that is a
deliberate choice rather than an admission of defeat.

WHAT IT COSTS

$6.40 a foot for conduit, clips and
weathering.

WHY NOT INSIDE

Because inside means through the insulation, through the vapour control, and
through a bay somebody will want to open later.

And because the thing a service usually connects to -- a solar panel, a tank,
a second building -- is outside anyway. A line that goes out at the apex and
down the outside crosses the envelope once. A line routed internally crosses
it twice and does the second crossing somewhere less convenient.

HOW IT LOOKS

Like conduit on the outside of a building, which is to say, industrial.

Some people mind. The honest answer is that the alternative is worse and the
conduit can be painted the colour of the shell, which is what the reference
build does.

THE PANELS IT FEEDS

Utility panels -- the reference build calls them polyps -- bolt to the
outside of the dome and take their service from this routing. A wall port at
$88 and the service connection at
$95.

Each one is a bathroom, a kitchen, a plant room or a battery bank hung on the
outside of the shell, fed from the top, occupying none of the floor.

That is what the exterior routing is for. It is not tidying-up; it is the
delivery mechanism for everything the building becomes later.

sections.title: Gasketed interface penetrations
sections.body:
A penetration is a hole with a promise attached, and the promise is what
costs money.

THE THREE THIS BUILDING HAS

The floor port, where everything arrives.

The apex sleeve, where everything leaves.

The wall ports, where utility panels connect.

That is it. Three kinds of hole in the entire envelope, all of them designed,
none of them cut later.

WHY GASKETED AND NOT SEALED

A sealed penetration is permanent. A gasketed one comes apart.

Every one of these three is somewhere the building expects to be opened: the
floor port when the dome moves, the apex cap when a service is added, the
wall port when a panel is swapped. Sealant at those points has to be cut out
and remade every time, which means it will not be, and the thing will be
open.

A gasket compresses when the fitting is done up and springs back when it is
undone. It can be done a hundred times and the hundredth is as good as the
first.

WHAT MAKES A GASKET WORK

Compression, evenly. That means a fitting that clamps rather than one that
is screwed down at one edge.

A face to compress against that is flat and clean. On a curved shell that
means a flange, and the flange is the expensive part.

And a groove for the gasket to sit in, so it cannot roll out under
compression. A gasket squeezed between two flat faces will find its way out.

THE FAILURE TO KNOW ABOUT

Gaskets take a set. A gasket left compressed for years does not spring back
as far, and a joint that has been open and shut a dozen times wants a new
one.

They cost a few dollars. Keep spares, and change them when the building is
open anyway.

sections.title: Replaceable service connections
sections.body:
Every service in this building is meant to be disconnected, and designing for
that is what makes the rest of the method possible.

THE PRINCIPLE

Nothing is plumbed or wired in permanently. Everything lands on a connector.

Water on a union or a quick-connect. Waste on a slip joint. Electrical on a
plug or a terminal block rather than a spliced run. Each of those costs a few
dollars more than the permanent version and takes the same time to fit.

WHAT IT BUYS

The dome moves. The column comes out and goes into the next one --
$260, rated for
25 years of service.

A fault is isolated rather than hunted. A connector is a place you can test
either side of.

A part is replaced rather than repaired. The fitting that failed comes off
and a new one goes on, by somebody who is not a tradesman.

And an upgrade is an afternoon. Better pump, bigger tank, more circuits: all
of them land on the same connectors.

THE ARGUMENT AGAINST, WHICH IS REAL

A connector is a joint, and every joint is a place that can leak or work
loose. A permanently plumbed system has fewer failure points than a
demountable one, and that is simply true.

The trade is between fewer failures and easier fixes, and this building
chooses easier fixes -- because it is a building that expects to be altered,
and one that cannot be altered without a tradesman will not be.

THE DISCIPLINE THAT MAKES IT WORK

Label everything. Standardise the fittings so there are three sizes in the
building and not eleven. Keep the spares in the under-floor storage that is
already there.

None of that is clever. All of it is the difference between a demountable
building and a building somebody once took apart and could not put back.

chapters.title: 14. Environmental Control
chapters.body:
A hemisphere has about 41 percent less envelope than a box of the same floor area, which is the biggest thermal fact about this shape and the reason everything in this chapter is smaller than the equivalent for a conventional building.

The shape gives that back in one place: the upper third of a dome's wall faces the sky, so it behaves like roof in summer. Most of what follows is about spending the saving well and not losing it through the top.
chapters.notes:
CHAPTER GOAL: Build a practical, illustrated chapter covering 14. Environmental Control.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Insulation
sections.body:
A dome's advantage is that it has less outside than a box does. Its
disadvantage is that the outside it has is curved, and insulation comes flat.

THE SHAPE ARGUMENT, FIRST

For the same floor area, a hemisphere has substantially less envelope than a
rectangular building -- the reference build's own model puts it at 41 percent
less.

That is real and it is the single biggest thermal thing about this shape.
Less surface means less heat leaving, before anybody has installed anything.

It also means the insulation you do buy goes further, because there is less
of it to buy.

THE STACK

Bare, the reference build's skin is about R-1.5. That is panels,
a membrane and the air films, and it is nearly nothing -- it is a tent with
opinions.

Each quilted layer adds about R-1.6. Seven of them reach
R-12.7, which is a real wall.

TWO WAYS TO BUY IT

In the bays, behind the panels. The frame gives six inches of cavity for
free, because the wedge's inward face stands proud of where the panel sits.
Fill it and it is done.

Or over the frame, under the cap. This is the reference build's route:
quilted recycled clothing, sewn by the owner, at a declared
$50 a layer.

The difference matters. A bay holds 4 layers and then it is full.
A cap is a bag -- every layer makes the next cap a size up, and there is no
limit. Seven layers makes the cap 15.6 percent bigger and nothing else
changes.

That is why this method insulates outside. Not because it performs better --
at the same R it does not -- but because it can keep going.

THE DEFERMENT ARGUMENT

Insulation bought a layer at a time is insulation bought when there is money.

The building works at R-1.5. Badly, in January. But it works,
and every winter after that it is warmer, and nothing has to come apart for
that to happen.

sections.title: Condensation
sections.body:
This is the failure mode most likely to ruin a building like this one, and
the reference build has an unproven answer to it. Both halves of that
sentence matter.

THE PHYSICS, BRIEFLY

Warm air holds more water than cold air. Inside air in an occupied building
is warm and wet -- people, cooking, washing, breathing.

That air moves outward through the envelope. Somewhere in the thickness of
the wall it reaches a temperature where it cannot hold its water any more,
and the water comes out as liquid.

That place is the dew point, and it moves depending on the weather.

WHY THIS BUILDING IS EXPOSED

The reference build's shower cap is a plastic membrane, then quilted fabric,
then a rain-slick cap.

Two impermeable layers with fabric between them is a moisture trap. Water
arrives in the fabric, cannot get out through either side, and stays. Wet
insulation does not insulate and wet fabric against timber rots it.

That is said out loud in the campaign film, on camera, because it is a real
objection and pretending otherwise would be dishonest.

THE ANSWER, AND ITS STATUS

The seam network.

Every interior seam of a wedge dome is a wedge-shaped channel -- 309 feet of
it, reaching every vertex, connecting all forty bays. Blow air through it and
the frame stays dry. Draw air through it and what condenses gets taken down
into a tank.

It is a duct that the geometry gives you free, and it is exactly the right
shape for this problem.

It is also unproven. Nobody has built it and measured it. The reference build
prices the fans and ports and says plainly that the performance is an
expectation rather than a measurement.

WHAT TO DO IN THE MEANTIME

Ventilate generously. Vent moisture at source -- a cooker hood, a bathroom
fan -- because air that never gets wet cannot deposit water in a wall.

And if you build this before anybody has measured the duct, open a bay in
spring and look.

sections.title: Ventilation
sections.body:
A small, tight, well-insulated building needs deliberate ventilation, and a
round one needs it more than most.

WHY MORE

A dome has no corners and no natural cross-draught. Air in a sphere wants to
circulate in a loop rather than pass through, and a room with one opening
does not ventilate at all -- it just breathes slowly at that opening.

Two openings, at different heights and on opposite sides, is the minimum that
produces actual airflow.

THE STACK EFFECT IS YOUR FRIEND HERE

Warm air rises, and a dome's highest point is dead centre and nine feet up.

An opening at the apex and an opening low at the perimeter gives you a
chimney: warm air leaves at the top, cool air is drawn in at the bottom, and
it happens without a fan for as long as there is a temperature difference.

That is free ventilation and it comes from the shape.

THE APEX IS ALREADY A HOLE

The seal cap is the obvious place for a controllable vent, and it costs
almost nothing to make it one.

THE SEAM DUCT, AGAIN

Reversible airflow through the seam network is the reference build's
ambition: blow to keep the frame dry, draw to collect what lands on the
shell.

Unproven, as the last section said. But the ports and the fans are priced,
the channel exists whether it is used or not, and a building that has the
ducting in it can experiment later.

THE RULE

Ventilation is not the same as draughts, and insulating a building without
ventilating it is how you get mould.

Tight envelope, deliberate openings, controllable. In that order.

sections.title: Heating
sections.body:
A small dome is easy to heat and easy to overheat, and the second is more
common.

HOW LITTLE IT TAKES

At R-12.7 with 277 square feet of floor, the heat load is small
enough that most domestic heaters are oversized for it.

That is not a boast; it is a warning. An oversized heater cycles -- full
blast, off, cold, full blast -- and a building with almost no thermal mass
follows it exactly. The room is alternately too hot and too cold and never
comfortable.

THE WOOD STOVE ARGUMENT

The reference build prices a small wood stove, and it suits this building for
reasons beyond the obvious.

It is mass, in a building that has none. A stove and its shield hold heat and
give it back slowly, which is the smoothing the envelope cannot do.

It is independent of the grid, which matters on the kind of land this
building goes on.

And its flue leaves through the apex, which is already a designed
penetration, so it does not cut a new hole.

The cost is floor area and a clearance zone, in a room that has 277 square
feet of it.

THE ALTERNATIVES

Electric resistance: cheapest to install, dearest to run, trivial to control.

Heat pump: dearest to install, cheapest to run, and the same unit does the
cooling.

Radiant, in the floor: only really available if the foundation is a slab,
which is one more thing the slab quietly buys.

THE DOME-SHAPED PROBLEM

A curved ceiling focuses. Heat rising from a stove in the middle collects at
the apex, and the apex is nine feet up where nobody is.

A slow ceiling fan pushing down solves it, and the reference build prices a
central light and fan as one fitting for that reason.

sections.title: Cooling
sections.body:
The dome's shape helps in winter and hurts in summer, and it is worth being
straight about which.

WHAT THE MODEL SAYS

The reference build sizes a window unit at a computed 3,365 BTU/h and buys a
6,000 BTU/h one, because that is the smallest thing actually sold.

Design temperature difference 20 degrees, solar
gain 2.6 BTU/h per square foot of glazing,
SEER 14.

Three thousand BTU is very small. A single room in a conventional house is
often twice that. The 41 percent envelope saving is doing most of the work.

THE SUMMER PROBLEM THE SHAPE CREATES

Upper panels face the sky.

In a box, the roof is the only surface facing up and it is the one everybody
insulates hardest. In a dome, the upper third of the *wall* faces up too, and
it is getting sun for the whole day rather than for the part of it when the
sun is on that side.

That is the real summer penalty of this shape and it does not get talked
about much.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS

Shade the top, which the next two sections are about.

Ventilate at night, when the outside air is cooler than the building, and
shut it up during the day. In a building with this little mass that works
less well than it does in a stone house, but it is free.

Do not glaze the top. A glazed upper bay is a skylight, it will light the
room beautifully, and it will cook it from May to September.

THE THING THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE

A dome is a reflector. A curved glazed surface facing a room concentrates
light and heat toward the centre, and in a nineteen-foot dome the centre is
where you are standing.

Two or three glazed bays are pleasant. Eight is a greenhouse, and it will
behave like one.

sections.title: Solar gain
sections.body:
Solar gain is heat arriving through glass, and in this shape it needs
counting rather than guessing.

THE NUMBER

2.6 BTU/h per square foot of glazing is
what the reference build's cooling model allows.

Multiply by the glazed area and you have the summer penalty in the same units
as the heater and the cooler. Three glazed bays at roughly 15 square feet
each is 45 square feet, which is about 117 BTU/h -- small. Ten bays is 390,
which is a meaningful fraction of the whole cooling load.

That is the calculation, and it takes a minute.

WHICH BAYS

Low bays face outward and give a view. Their gain is seasonal and modest,
because in summer the sun is high and strikes them at a glancing angle.

Upper bays face the sky. Their gain is worst exactly when you least want it,
because in summer the sun is high and strikes them square on.

That is the whole geometry of it, and it is why the answer to "where should
the windows go" is *low*.

THE WINTER SIDE OF THE LEDGER

Solar gain is free heat in January.

A dome with glazing on its equator-facing side collects usefully in winter,
when the sun is low and strikes those panels square. The same panels that are
glancing in July are perpendicular in December.

So: glazing low on the sun side is good twice. Glazing high is bad once and
good never.

THE HONEST LIMIT

None of this is a substitute for a real energy model. It is enough to stop
somebody putting eight glass triangles in the roof because it looked good in
a render.

sections.title: Shading
sections.body:
Shading is the cheapest cooling there is and the one that suits this shape
best, because the surface you need to shade is the one you were going to put
something over anyway.

THE CAP IS ALREADY THERE

The reference build's outer layer is a rain-slick cap strapped over the
building.

Its colour is a free decision and it is worth making deliberately. A light
cap reflects; a dark cap absorbs. On a surface this size that is a
substantial difference in summer and a small one in winter, because winter
sun is low and weak.

Light, unless there is a specific reason.

EXTERNAL BEATS INTERNAL, ALWAYS

A blind inside a window stops light after it has already entered the
building. The heat is in the room; the blind only decides where it lands.

Anything outside stops the heat before it arrives. An external shade is
several times more effective than an internal one and it is the
straightforward thing people skip because internal blinds are easier to buy.

WHAT SUITS A DOME

A brise-soleil over the upper bays: a panel standing off the shell,
shading the glass and letting air move behind it.

Deciduous trees. Shade in summer, bare branches in winter, and the site
probably has some. This is the best shading device available and it costs
nothing if you site the building thoughtfully.

A removable panel over a glazed bay. This one is specific to the method: the
bays are demountable, so a glazed bay can become a solid bay for the summer
and back again in October. That is twenty minutes with a driver.

THE SHADING THE SHAPE GIVES YOU FREE

A dome shades itself. The curve means one side is always turned away from the
sun, and the transition is gradual rather than the hard shadow line a box
casts on itself.

sections.title: Moisture management
sections.body:
The whole of environmental control in this building comes down to where the
water is, so this section collects what the others have been circling.

THE FOUR PLACES WATER ARRIVES

Rain, on the outside. Handled by the cap and by the seams -- shed, do not
seal, two lines of defence rather than one.

Ground, from below. Handled by the pad, the drainage and a membrane under the
floor. 40 inches a year is what the reference build
assumes falls, and all of it has to go somewhere that is not under the
building.

Occupants, from inside. Cooking, washing, breathing. Handled by ventilation
at source.

Condensation, in the middle of the wall. Handled by -- as the section on it
says -- an unproven duct, and until somebody measures it, by generous
ventilation and by looking.

THE ORDER OF PRIORITY

Keep it out. Cheapest, most effective, and where nearly all the effort
belongs.

Let it escape. A wall that can dry in both directions forgives a lot. A wall
sealed on both faces forgives nothing, which is the shower cap's structural
weakness as a design.

Manage what is left. Fans, dehumidifiers, and opening a window.

THE CATCHMENT, WHICH TURNS THE PROBLEM AROUND

A dome is an excellent rainwater catchment: a smooth curved surface, one low
edge all the way round, and a seam network that already reaches every part of
it.

The reference build assumes 72 percent of what
falls can be caught. On this footprint, with
40 inches a year, that is thousands of gallons.

Which is the useful way to think about the whole chapter. The water is going
to arrive regardless. The only question is whether the building is arranged
to get rid of it or arranged to keep it.

chapters.title: 15. Variations of the Wedge Method
chapters.body:
The wedge is a sector of a log, and the reason the method works is that the 45-degree sector you split out of a tree is exactly the seam budget the dome needs -- both pairs of seam angles sum to 45 degrees.

Everything in this chapter is a way of making that member some other way, and each one trades a piece of that argument for something else. It is worth knowing which piece.
chapters.notes:

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: Solid wedges
sections.body:
A solid wedge is one piece of timber, sawn to a triangular section, and it is
what this whole method assumes unless something says otherwise.

WHAT IT IS

A sector of a log. Split a round log into 8 radial pieces and each
one is a 45-degree wedge -- flat on two faces, curved on the third,
and pointed along one edge.

The reference build's member is
4.59 inches across the wide face and
6.0 inches deep.

WHY THE SHAPE IS THE POINT

Two sawn faces meeting at an angle is a joint you can make with a saw.

The 45-degree sector is not arbitrary: it is the whole seam budget
of the dome. The A seams fold 18.029 degrees and open 26.971; the B seams fold
22.459 and open 22.541. Both pairs sum to 45, which is the raw
sector you split out of the tree.

That is the closest thing this method has to a theorem, and it is why a split
log is the right stock for this building rather than a convenient one.

THE ADVANTAGES

Strength. One piece of continuous grain, no glue line, no fastener in the
section.

Cost. It is what comes out of a tree. There is no processing between the
splitting and the using.

Simplicity. Nothing to delaminate, nothing to come apart, nothing that needs
a shop.

THE LIMITS

Size. The member cannot be bigger than the log. Two trees give
160 members where the dome needs
120, which is comfortable at this size and would not be at
twice it.

Movement. Solid timber moves as it dries, and a wedge sawn green will not be
the same wedge in a year. Build green and accept the movement, or dry and
accept the wait.

Defects. A knot in a solid member is a weakness in that member. There is no
lamination to spread the load round it.

sections.title: Hollow members
sections.body:
A hollow member is a box: four thin walls enclosing air, in the same outside
shape as the solid one.

THE ARGUMENT FOR

Stiffness lives near the surface. In bending, the material at the middle of a
section is doing very little, and taking it out costs less strength than it
saves weight.

At 15.3 square inches of solid section, a hollow
equivalent might use half the material for most of the stiffness.

The frame weighs 2,478 pounds in green pine. Halving that changes what two
people can lift, which changes how the dome gets built.

THE ARGUMENT AGAINST, WHICH IS DECISIVE HERE

You cannot make one with a saw.

A hollow triangular member is four pieces, ripped accurately, glued or
fastened along four long joints, in a jig, by somebody with a shop. That is
the exact work the wedge method exists to avoid.

And the whole harvest advantage disappears. The method's economy comes from
using 88 percent of a trunk instead of the 45 percent a mill gets. A hollow
member is made from milled boards, so it starts from the 45.

WHERE IT WOULD MAKE SENSE

A manufactured dome, in a factory, where the jig is a fixed cost spread over
hundreds of frames and the weight saving compounds through shipping.

Not for somebody with a chainsaw and two trees.

THE MIDDLE OPTION NOBODY TRIES

Solid wedges with the middle bored out along the length. It keeps the sawn
faces, keeps the continuous grain at the surface, and removes some of the
weight.

It is fiddly, it needs a long auger, and nobody has measured what it does.
Listed here as an idea rather than a recommendation.

sections.title: Laminated wedges
sections.body:
A laminated wedge is built up from thinner pieces glued face to face, then
cut to the wedge section.

WHAT IT BUYS

Size beyond the tree. A laminated member can be any length and any section,
which removes the constraint that the log sets.

Straightness. Laminating averages out the movement in each lamina, and a
glued-up member stays where you put it in a way a solid one does not.

Defects spread. A knot in one lamina is surrounded by six that are clear, so
its effect on the whole is small. That is why glulam is graded higher than
the timber it is made from.

Grain direction, chosen. You can put the strong direction where the load is.

WHAT IT COSTS

Boards, which means milling, which means the 45 percent recovery rather than
the 88.

Glue, clamps, a flat surface long enough, and the time for it to cure.

And a level of shop practice that most of this book is written to avoid
needing.

WHERE IT EARNS ITS PLACE

Big domes. Above a certain span the member a tree can give you is not enough,
and lamination is the only way to keep going with timber.

Long-span headers over openings, where one member is carrying what several
used to.

And repairs: a failed member replaced with a laminated one, because the right
tree is not standing there today.

THE HONEST POSITION

Lamination is better engineering and worse economics, and this method is an
economic argument. It belongs in the book because at some sizes there is no
alternative -- not because it is an upgrade to reach for at this one.

sections.title: Split wedges
sections.body:
Splitting is different from sawing, and the difference is the oldest argument
in woodworking.

SPLIT VERSUS SAWN

A saw cuts through the fibres wherever the blade goes. A split follows them.

Split stock is therefore stronger along its length, because no fibre is cut
short -- which is why axe handles and riven oak gates are split, and why a
sawn one of the same dimensions breaks first.

It is also faster and needs no power.

WHAT IT COSTS

Accuracy. A split follows the grain, and the grain in a real tree is not
perfectly straight. A split wedge is approximately the shape you wanted, and
the amount of approximately depends on the tree.

Kerf, though: none. The reference build's model loses
51.2 board feet per log to a
0.25-inch kerf -- out of 442 solid --
and splitting loses none of it.

THE METHOD THAT ACTUALLY WORKS

Split radially, into 8 pieces, then clean the two faces that
matter with a saw or a plane.

That gets the strength of split stock and the accuracy of sawn faces on the
two surfaces that have to mate. The curved back is left as it comes, because
nothing bears on it.

That is the reference build's assumption and it is the reason the numbers
work: it is a split log with two tidied faces, not a machined beam.

WHERE IT FAILS

Twisted grain. Some trees spiral, and a spiral log splits into spiral wedges.
Test one section before committing sixty feet.

Big knots. A split runs into a knot and goes round it, or stops.

Species. Straight-grained softwoods split beautifully. Interlocked tropical
hardwoods do not split at all.

sections.title: Log-derived wedges
sections.body:
This is the reference build, and it is worth setting out as a variation
rather than as the default, because the numbers only work for a particular
kind of tree.

THE LOG THE MODEL ASSUMES

15 inches at the butt,
5.5 at the top,
60 feet usable, cut into
12-foot sections.

That is an ordinary plantation softwood. Not a veteran, not a specimen, not
anything anybody would object to felling.

WHAT ONE GIVES YOU

442 board feet solid. Take off
51.2 for kerf and 391 board feet end up in
wedges -- 40 of them, making 80 struts at
4.89 board feet each.

Two trees make 160 members. The dome needs
120. So a 2V hemisphere of this size is two trees, with a
third of the stock spare for mistakes.

THE COMPARISON THAT MATTERS

Milled, the same log yields about 45 percent of itself as usable lumber. The
rest is slab, edging and sawdust.

Split into wedges, it yields about 88 percent. Nothing is edged because
nothing needs a rectangular section.

That is a 1.95x harvest advantage. Against it, the pinwheel frame uses 1.80x
more stock than a mitred one, because every joint overlaps rather than
meeting. Net: a wedge dome uses about 92 percent of the trees a mitred dome
of the same size would.

Eight percent, which is small -- and the point was never the eight percent.
It is that the eight percent comes with no mitre saw, no jig, no shop, and a
log instead of a lumber order.

THE CONSTRAINTS TO CHECK BEFORE COUNTING ON IT

Straight grain, adequate diameter, and enough of them. A stand of crooked
scrub will not do this, however many stems it has.

sections.title: Manufactured wedges
sections.body:
A manufactured wedge is one made to a specification, in quantity, by somebody
else -- and it is the version of this method that could actually be sold.

WHAT CHANGES

Consistency. Every member identical to a thousandth, which makes everything
downstream easier: panels that fit, snap fittings that work, assembly
instructions that are true.

Grading. Stress-graded stock with a number on it, which is what an engineer
needs and what a building inspector will ask for.

Treatment. Pressure treatment, fire retardant, or preservative, applied
properly rather than brushed on.

Species choice. The right timber rather than the one growing on the site.

WHAT IS LOST

The tree. The method's central economic claim -- your frame is already
standing on your land -- does not survive being bought in a bundle.

The recovery advantage. A factory making rectangular-ish stock into wedges
starts from milled lumber and the 45 percent.

The independence. A manufactured wedge is a supply chain.

THE HONEST ASSESSMENT

Manufactured wedges make a better product and a worse argument.

For a kit sold to somebody who wants a dome and does not want a chainsaw,
they are obviously right. For the person this book is mostly addressed to --
somebody with land, trees and time, and not much money -- they remove the
only reason the method was interesting.

Both markets are real. They are not the same market, and a design that tries
to serve both usually serves neither.

sections.title: Hybrid metal/wood systems
sections.body:
Steel where the strength is and timber everywhere else is a sound principle
and the reference build already uses it in one place.

WHERE IT ALREADY APPEARS

The mast: a steel core running the height of the utility column, clad in
timber.

The floor: a steel hub clamping that mast, steel spokes radiating to the base
ring, timber decking over them.

In both cases the metal is doing a job timber is bad at -- carrying a
concentrated load through a small section -- and the timber is doing the job
metal is expensive at, which is covering area.

WHERE ELSE IT WOULD WORK

A steel base ring. The ring is a compression ring, it works in pure hoop
stress, and that is exactly what a steel band is for. It would also stop the
ring being the thing that limits how many openings you can cut.

Steel connectors at high-load vertices. The apex, and the base vertices where
the dome delivers its load to the pad.

Steel headers over openings.

WHERE IT WOULD NOT

Everywhere. A steel-framed dome is a different building with different
economics, and it loses the harvest argument entirely.

THE JOINT IS THE PROBLEM

Timber moves and steel does not.

A timber member bolted rigidly to a steel plate will, over a few seasons of
shrinking and swelling, either crush around the bolt or split from it. The
fix is a connection that allows movement in the direction timber moves --
slotted holes, or a single central fastener rather than a rigid pattern of
them.

That is well understood and routinely got wrong.

CORROSION

Wet timber and steel together is a battery. Use stainless or hot-dip
galvanised at every point where the two meet, and particularly at the base,
where water collects.

The reference build specifies stainless throughout its bolted connections,
which costs more and removes a whole category of failure from the building's
future.

chapters.title: 16. Different Dome Configurations
chapters.body:
Frequency decides how many pieces you cut. Where you cut the sphere decides what it is like to live in.

Most of the disappointment people report with domes comes from the second of those, and nearly all the writing about them is about the first.
chapters.notes:
CHAPTER GOAL: Build a practical, illustrated chapter covering 16. Different Dome Configurations.

Use the 20-foot 2V reference dome when a verified worked example helps. Keep tested construction, derived geometry, and untested possibilities visibly separate.

sections.title: 1V
sections.body:
A 1V dome is an icosahedron cut in half: twenty triangles on the whole
sphere, and every one of them identical.

WHAT IT IS GOOD FOR

Learning. One strut length, one triangle, one angle. You can build a model of
one in an evening out of drinking straws and understand more about geodesic
geometry than a week of reading will give you.

Cheapness. Fewer members, fewer joints, less of everything.

Speed. There is nothing to sort, because every piece is the same piece.

WHAT IT IS BAD AT

Being round. A 1V dome is visibly a faceted polyhedron, not a sphere. The
flat triangles are large relative to the building and the shape reads as
angular.

That matters structurally as well as visually: a large flat panel in a shell
carries bending that a smaller, more curved arrangement would resolve as
membrane action.

Headroom. The facets cut in aggressively, so the usable floor is a smaller
fraction of the footprint than in a higher frequency.

WHERE IT ACTUALLY BELONGS

Small structures. A greenhouse, a play structure, a chicken house, a shed.
At small spans the faceting does not matter and the simplicity is everything.

And as the first thing anybody builds. Build a 1V, in a weekend, before
committing to something that takes a month. Everything you learn transfers.

sections.title: 2V
sections.body:
The 2V is the reference build and the shape the rest of this book assumes.

WHAT IT IS

Each face of the icosahedron divided into four, giving 80 triangles on the
sphere and 40 faces on the hemisphere --
10 of one kind and 30 of the other.

Two strut lengths, A and B, rather than one.

WHY IT IS THE SWEET SPOT

Two lengths is manageable. You can sort two piles in your head; five you
cannot, and above that people start colour-coding and still get it wrong.

It is round enough. The faceting is visible but not dominant.

It is big enough to live in. The reference build is a
19.42-foot sphere cut at the equator --
296 square feet inside the circle, or
277 inside the ten-sided figure the base ring
actually makes.

And the parts count is buildable by hand: 26 vertices,
120 members, 55 interior seams and
10 base edges.

THE NUMBERS THAT DEFINE IT

Radius 116.4984 inches. The A chord is 72.000 inches
and the B chord 63.6703.

Note what that does not say. The chord is the distance between two vertices;
the *stock* you cut is neither. An A member is
70.182 inches of timber against a
72-inch chord, because a pinwheel member runs past the
vertex rather than stopping at it.

Confusing the chord with the cut is the most expensive mistake available in
this method, and it is available on the very first cut.

Dihedral angles fall between 157.5 and
162.0 degrees -- a spread of under five degrees
across the whole building, which is why one gasket thickness works
everywhere. That is topology, so it holds at any diameter.

309 feet of interior seam, reaching every vertex.

THE THING IT DOES NOT SOLVE

No panel of a 2V at this size fits a four-foot sheet.

The AAA faces are 62.354 inches across their narrowest
altitude and the BAB faces 52.516. A sheet is 48. The
narrowest panel in the building is four and a half inches too wide, in every
rotation.

That is entirely a consequence of picking this frequency at this diameter. A
different diameter moves it, and this one was picked for a six-foot member
rather than for a sheet of plywood.

sections.title: 3V
sections.body:
A 3V divides each icosahedral face into nine, giving 180 triangles on the
sphere.

WHAT IT BUYS

Roundness. A 3V reads as a sphere rather than as a polyhedron, and the
difference at any size above a shed is obvious.

Smaller panels, which means sheet goods start to fit, which quietly solves
the 2V's sheet problem.

Better structural behaviour. More, smaller triangles distribute load more
evenly and rely less on any single member.

And a proper base. A 3V can be cut at several heights, including one that
gives a near-vertical lower wall -- which is the thing people most often want
from a dome and cannot get from a 2V.

WHAT IT COSTS

Three strut lengths, and the member count roughly triples from the reference
build's 120. That is three piles to keep straight and
three times as many joints to make.

More seams, more gaskets, more sealing, more of every per-joint cost.

And at this scale the wedge method starts to strain: a hundred and twenty
members is a weekend of sorting and four hundred is a different kind of job.

WHERE THE LINE IS

Roughly: up to about 20 feet, 2V. From about 25 feet upward, 3V. Between
them it is a judgement about whether you would rather cut more pieces or live
in a more faceted room.

The reference build sits at 19.4 feet, just under the line, which is
not a coincidence.

THE WEDGE-SPECIFIC CATCH

A higher frequency means shorter members, and shorter members mean the
pinwheel overlap is a larger fraction of each one.

At the reference build's size an A member is
70.2 inches of stock for a
72-inch chord. Halve the chord and the overlap does not
halve with it, so the ratio gets worse.

The pinwheel already carries a 1.80x stock penalty against a mitred frame,
covered by a 1.95x harvest advantage. As the members get shorter that
penalty grows and at some frequency the harvest stops covering it.

Nobody has worked out where. It is one of the open questions this book would
rather name than paper over.

sections.title: Hemispheres
sections.body:
A hemisphere is a sphere cut at its equator, and it is the default for good
reasons and one bad one.

THE GOOD REASONS

It sits flat. The cut is a plane, the base is a circle, and the building
lands on level ground without anything below it.

It is the most enclosed volume per unit of surface of anything you can build.
That is where the 41 percent envelope saving over a box comes from.

The base ring is a compression ring. Cut at the equator, the ring is in pure
hoop stress, which is the most efficient thing a ring can be doing. Cut above
or below and there is a vertical component the ring has to resolve.

The maths is clean. Strut lengths and angles for hemispheres are published;
a cut anywhere else has to be solved.

THE BAD REASON

Habit. Most domes are hemispheres because most domes are hemispheres.

WHAT A HEMISPHERE IS ACTUALLY LIKE TO BE IN

The reference build is 19.42 feet across and 9.708 feet to
the apex. The floor inside the base ring is
277 square feet.

That sounds generous and in the middle it is. At the perimeter the wall is
leaning in hard: a hemisphere's surface is 45 degrees from vertical at
half its height, so by the time you are at head height near the edge, the
usable floor is well inside the footprint.

So the floor area a hemisphere gives you and the floor area you can stand
upright on are different numbers, and the second is the one that matters.

It is the first thing people are disappointed by, and it is the reason the
next three sections exist.

sections.title: Partial spheres
sections.body:
A partial sphere is cut somewhere other than the equator, and which way you
cut changes the building completely.

CUT BELOW THE EQUATOR

More than half a sphere. The walls come back in below the widest point, so
the floor is smaller than the widest part of the building.

Nobody does this deliberately for a house -- you lose floor and gain an
overhang that has to be supported. It appears in water tanks and in
structures where the enclosed volume is the point rather than the floor.

CUT ABOVE THE EQUATOR

Less than half a sphere: a shallow cap. More floor for the height, a lower
profile, less material.

This is a good shape for something that does not need headroom at the
perimeter -- a workshop with benches round the edge, a store, a cover over
something. It sheds snow less well and it is less stable in wind, because
there is less depth to resist overturning.

THE TRADE, PLAINLY

Cut low and you get a tall building with a small floor. Cut high and you get
a wide building with a low ceiling. The equator is the balance and that is
most of why it is the default.

THE STRUCTURAL CATCH

A cut above the equator has a base ring that is not in pure hoop stress. The
shell above it leans outward, so the ring is being pushed out as well as
squeezed, and it needs either more section or a tie across the floor.

A ring beam and a tension ring in the floor deck handle it. It is not
difficult. It is just not free, and the hemisphere gets it free.

sections.title: Knee-wall domes
sections.body:
A knee wall is a short vertical wall between the foundation and the dome, and
it is the single most effective change you can make to how a dome feels
inside.

WHAT IT FIXES

The lean. Every complaint about living in a dome is a complaint about the
perimeter -- furniture that will not go against a wall, a door you duck
through, a room whose usable area is smaller than its floor.

Raise the shell three feet on a vertical wall and all of those improve at
once. The wall is vertical where furniture is, the door is a normal door, and
the usable floor grows by more than the wall's own area.

WHAT IT COSTS

The wall itself, which is conventional construction and cheap.

Some of the shape's efficiency: more envelope for the same floor, so the
41 percent saving shrinks.

And the base ring stops being the dome's ring. The dome now lands on a wall,
and the wall has to resolve the outward thrust the ring used to take in hoop
stress. That means a top plate acting as a ring beam, properly joined at
every splice, and a tie across the floor or a foundation stiff enough to
resist spreading.

That last point is the one that gets missed. A dome on a knee wall is pushing
that wall outward all the time, and the wall is not a dome and cannot resolve
it by itself.

HOW HIGH

Two to four feet is the useful range.

Under two, it does not change the feel enough to be worth the complication.
Over four, the building stops reading as a dome and starts reading as a round
house with a domed roof -- which is a perfectly good building and a different
one.

THE HONEST RECOMMENDATION

If somebody is going to live in it full time, and they have not lived in a
dome before, a three-foot knee wall is probably the right answer and this
book's reference build does not have one.

sections.title: Raised domes
sections.body:
A raised dome is one lifted clear of the ground on posts, piers or -- in this
method's more speculative corner -- cables.

WHY

Flood. Getting the floor above water is the whole reason in some places.

Slope. A raised platform gets level out of ground that is not, without moving
earth.

Airflow underneath, which keeps a timber building dry.

The view, and the space beneath, which becomes storage, parking or shade.

WHAT IT DEMANDS

The platform becomes the structure. The dome above it is a shell that
resolves its own loads; the posts and beams below are a frame that racks and
must be braced in both directions.

Wind matters more. A raised building has more exposed area, and the
overturning moment is the wind load times the height -- so going up
compounds.

Access is a stair, and the stair is not an afterthought.

THE VERSION THIS METHOD REACHES FOR

Hung, not stood.

The reference build prices a mast through the utility column, a floor that
clamps to that mast, an apex lifting ring and three cables to saddles on two
trees. The rig is $1,490, the mast and floor are $4,011 together, against a
frame weighing 2,478 pounds.

Saddles, not holes: nothing is drilled into the trees.

THE SENTENCE THAT HAS TO GO WITH IT

That is a design possibility, not an engineered structure.

The loads on the trees, the cables and the mast need an engineer before
anybody stands under it. The model prices the parts; it does not rate them,
and the difference between those two things is the whole of somebody's
safety.

author_voice_instructions:
THE WEDGE METHOD - AUTHOR / LLM WRITING INSTRUCTIONS

Purpose
This project is a practical construction and design book about timber geodesic domes, the wedge method, its geometry, fabrication, assembly, enclosure, utility interfaces, and variations. Add useful content to the book without changing the author's voice or turning it into generic AI prose.

Author voice
- Write like a builder, fabricator, programmer, and technical problem-solver explaining a system to another capable person.
- Prefer direct language over academic language.
- Explain what a part does before introducing equations or jargon.
- Use concrete dimensions, examples, diagrams, cut logic, and practical consequences wherever possible.
- Short paragraphs are preferred. Use tables when dimensions or options are easier to compare visually.
- It is acceptable to say "we" when walking the reader through a construction process. Use "I" only when the project notes explicitly document that the author personally built, measured, tested, observed, or decided something.
- Do not write marketing fluff, inspirational filler, canned introductions, fake quotations, or phrases such as "in today's rapidly evolving world," "delve," "game changer," "revolutionary," or "it is important to note."
- Do not repeatedly summarize what was just said. Move the construction logic forward.
- The prose should read like it was written and revised by the book's human author, not like a chatbot transcript.

Technical integrity
- Never invent measurements, test results, load ratings, wind ratings, snow ratings, span capacity, fastener capacity, code compliance, engineering approval, material properties, or personal build history.
- Never claim that an experimental configuration is structurally safe simply because the geometry can be drawn.
- Separate information into these categories when appropriate:
  GEOMETRY - mathematically derived relationships.
  BUILD NOTE - documented fabrication or assembly experience.
  DESIGN VARIATION - a plausible modification of the basic method.
  EXPERIMENTAL - an idea requiring testing, calculation, or engineering validation.
  SAFETY / ENGINEERING - information where loads, code, electrical, plumbing, fire, soil, foundation, occupancy, or professional review matters.
- If source information conflicts, do not silently choose one. Flag the conflict in development notes.
- Show units and preserve unit conversions. For builder-facing dimensions, inches and feet should be readable as fractions or decimals appropriate to the operation.
- Distinguish nominal lumber dimensions from actual dressed dimensions.
- State assumptions used in calculations.
- Whenever a dimension is derived from dome frequency, truncation, radius, diameter, or sphere geometry, identify the geometry being assumed.

Sources and citations
- Do not fabricate citations.
- When a technical claim needs external support, insert a development-note marker in this format:
  [SOURCE NEEDED: concise description of claim]
- Keep quoted material minimal. Prefer paraphrase and cite the original source.
- Building-code requirements must be tied to a specific jurisdiction and code edition if they are stated as requirements.

How to add a new section
1. Read the chapter goal and development notes first.
2. Identify whether the section is geometry, tested construction, design variation, experimental design, or safety/engineering.
3. Draft the practical explanation first.
4. Add equations only where they help the reader calculate or fabricate something.
5. Add a worked example if the section contains a calculation.
6. Add figure recommendations in development notes using:
   [FIGURE: description]
7. Add table recommendations using:
   [TABLE: description]
8. Add missing research needs using:
   [SOURCE NEEDED: description]
9. Never fabricate an author's personal anecdote to make the text sound human.
10. Preserve the author's existing terminology unless a correction is technically necessary; if so, explain the correction in development notes rather than silently rewriting the conceptual system.

Reference build
The manuscript uses a 20-foot-diameter 2V dome as a recurring reference build. Use it to make abstract geometry concrete, but do not assume dimensions that have not been calculated and verified for the exact 2V configuration used by the book.

Book organization
The reader should be able to move through this sequence:
geometry -> wedge fabrication -> strut fabrication -> connections -> base layout -> dome assembly -> openings -> shell/panels -> foundations/floor -> utilities -> environmental control -> variations -> modular systems -> applications -> reference designs -> builder tables.

Editing rule
When revising existing text, preserve useful technical detail. Do not "simplify" by removing dimensions, assumptions, exceptions, warnings, or construction logic. If something is wrong, correct it and record the reason in development notes.
production_elements:
BOOK BUILD-OUT ELEMENTS

Core format
- Working title: The Wedge Method
- Subtitle: A Builder's Guide to Timber Geodesic Domes
- Subject: geometry, fabrication, assembly, enclosure, utilities, and variations of the timber wedge method
- Primary print target: 8.5 x 11 inch paperback manual
- Reference build: 20-foot-diameter 2V dome
- Draft target length: approximately 180-300 illustrated pages

Information classes used throughout the manuscript
GEOMETRY - mathematically derived information.
BUILD NOTE - information supported by documented fabrication or assembly experience.
DESIGN VARIATION - a modification that can be derived from the basic system.
EXPERIMENTAL - a possibility requiring testing, calculation, or engineering validation.
SAFETY / ENGINEERING - information where loads, code, electrical, plumbing, fire, soil, foundation, occupancy, or professional review matters.

Recurring reference-build box
Use a clearly marked "REFERENCE BUILD - 20 FT 2V DOME" box whenever a chapter can show how an abstract concept applies to the reference structure. Exact dimensions must be calculated and verified before publication.

Illustration program
- Complete 2V dome
- Exploded 2V dome
- A-member highlighting
- B-member highlighting
- Two triangle families
- Wedge cross-section
- Conventional rectangular strut versus wedge strut
- Log divided into wedge members
- Dimensional-lumber wedge-cutting layouts
- Inward wedge orientation
- Three-member vertex
- Five-member vertex
- Six-member vertex where applicable
- Dihedral relationship
- Triangle-to-triangle joint
- Base attachment
- First course
- Second course
- Apex assembly
- Door opening
- Reinforced opening
- Removable panel
- Insulated panel
- Utility column
- Floor utility interface
- Apex utility interface
- Gasketed service cap
- Prepared dome pad
- Completed dome cutawayTables and worksheets to develop
- Verified 2V chord-factor table for the exact dome truncation used in the book
- Diameter-to-strut-length tables
- Triangle side and altitude tables
- Vertex/member-count tables
- Wedge cross-section and taper tables
- Cut-list worksheet
- Material-yield worksheet for logs and dimensional lumber
- Fastener schedule worksheet (project-specific; not universal engineering values)
- Panel dimensions and surface-area worksheets
- Floor-area and circumference tables
- Unit-conversion table
- Blank builder project sheet

Research / verification queue
- Verify all dome geometry against a reproducible mathematical source or derivation
- Define the exact 2V sphere subdivision and truncation used by the reference build
- Document the wedge angle and the relationship between wedge taper and face-to-face dome geometry
- Test and photograph representative joints
- Record real saw setups, jigs, cut sequence, tolerances, and measured error
- Record material species, nominal/actual dimensions, and moisture condition for physical examples
- Photograph or render assembly stages
- Separate concept renderings from tested builds
- Obtain reliable sources for structural-geometry background and material properties where used
- Treat building-code statements by jurisdiction and code edition rather than as universal rules
- Have structural claims intended for occupied buildings professionally reviewed before presenting them as construction specifications

Writing workflow
1. Develop geometry and terminology first.
2. Freeze the reference-dome definition.
3. Build verified strut/triangle tables.
4. Document the actual wedge-fabrication process.
5. Document joint alternatives and which ones were physically tested.
6. Write assembly chapters from actual build order.
7. Add shell, foundation, utility, and environmental-control systems.
8. Add design variations only after the baseline system is clear.
9. Add reference designs and builder worksheets last.

LLM handoff / upload workflow
